The Submodular Secretary Problem:
Tight 1−1/e1-1/e for Monotone Objectives,
and Strictly Between 1/e1/e and 1/21/2 in General

Hamed Abdi ††thanks: University of Maryland, College Park. Email: hamedabdi37@gmail.com.    Kiarash Banihashem ††thanks: University of Maryland, College Park. Email: kiarash@umd.edu.    MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi ††thanks: University of Maryland, College Park. Email: hajiaghayi@gmail.com.    Danny Mittal ††thanks: University of Maryland, College Park. Email: dannymittal@gmail.com.
November 2026
Abstract

In the submodular secretary problem with a cardinality constraint, nn elements arrive in uniformly random order, and an algorithm must irrevocably accept or reject each one on arrival so as to maximize a nonnegative submodular function over sets of at most kk elements. For monotone objectives we settle the problem: the optimal competitive ratio tends to exactly 1−1/e1-1/e as k→∞k\to\infty, and its worst case over all budgets kk is exactly 1/e1/e. The bound 1−1/e1-1/e cannot be exceeded even with unlimited computation, and it is achieved by a single algorithm with at most 4​n+14n+1 value queries; previously the best ratio without a shortlist was 1/e−o⁡(1)1/e-o(1), with exponentially many queries. For general objectives, where the best known ratio was about 0.1070.107, we show that the optimal limiting ratio lies strictly between 1/e1/e and 1/21/2: we achieve 1/e+3.5⋅10−61/e+3.5\cdot 10^{-6} for large kk, and no algorithm achieves more than 0.4970530.497053. We also achieve 0.26770.2677 at every budget. The main new ingredient of our algorithm is eligibility attenuation: an element that passes the price test at time tt is accepted with probability e−τe^{-\tau}, where τ\tau is the total earlier time during which it would have passed, which makes the probability that it has already been selected exactly 1−e−τ1-e^{-\tau}.

1 Introduction

In the classical secretary problem [Dyn63, Lin61], nn values are revealed in uniformly random order and we must stop at one of them, deciding irrevocably as each appears. Observing a 1/e1/e fraction of the values and then taking the next record selects the maximum with probability approaching 1/e1/e, which is optimal. Since the work of Hajiaghayi, Kleinberg, and Parkes [HKP04] and Kleinberg [Kle05], the random-order model has been used to study online selection of several elements, including under matroid constraints [BIK07, ABH+26].

When the objective has decreasing marginal values, the natural formulation is the submodular secretary problem, introduced independently by Bateni, Hajiaghayi, and Zadimoghaddam [BHZ13] and Gupta, Roth, Schoenebeck, and Talwar [GRST10]. We study its most basic constrained form. A ground set EE of nn elements arrives in uniformly random order, and the algorithm knows nn and an integer k≤nk\leq n. When an element arrives, the algorithm may query a nonnegative submodular function f:2E→ℝ≥0f:2^{E}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} on subsets of the elements that have arrived so far, and must then accept or reject the element immediately and irrevocably, accepting at most kk elements in total. Its competitive ratio is the infimum, over instances, of 𝔼⁡[f⁡(A)]/OPT\mathbb{E}[f(A)]/\mathrm{OPT}, where AA is the accepted set and OPT=max|S|≤k⁡f⁡(S)\mathrm{OPT}=\max_{|S|\leq k}f(S).

Offline, this problem has well-known benchmarks. For monotone ff, greedy achieves 1−(1−1/k)k≥1−1/e1-(1-1/k)^{k}\geq 1-1/e [NWF78], and no algorithm making polynomially many value queries does better asymptotically [NW78]. For general nonnegative ff, the measured continuous greedy algorithm achieves 1/e1/e [FNS11b]; this is a natural barrier for clean analyses, although more elaborate algorithms achieve slightly better constants [BFNS14, EN16, BF24]. Online, the known guarantees have remained far from these benchmarks. The ratio for monotone objectives improved from 0.0900.090 [BHZ13] to 0.1700.170 [FNS11a], and then Kesselheim and Tönnis [KT17] showed that repeatedly optimizing over the observed prefix gives 0.275−o⁡(1)0.275-o(1) in polynomial time and 1/e−o⁡(1)1/e-o(1) with exact, exponential-query optimization. For general objectives the best known ratios were 1/(8​e2)1/(8e^{2}) [BHZ13] and then (e−1)2/(e2​(1+e))≈0.107(e-1)^{2}/(e^{2}(1+e))\approx 0.107 [Fuj19]. Agrawal, Shadravan, and Stein [ASS19] reach 1−1/e−ε1-1/e-\varepsilon for monotone objectives, but only when the algorithm may keep a shortlist of O⁡(k)O(k) candidates and make its final choice afterwards.

This leaves two basic questions open. Does the ability to delay decisions, which a shortlist grants, matter for monotone objectives? And can the 1/e1/e offline benchmark for general objectives be matched online?

1.1 Main results

Our main result answers both questions with a single algorithm, AttenuatedPricing (Section 3). To state it uniformly, we say that ff is μ\mu-monotone, for μ∈[0,1]\mu\in[0,1], if f⁡(B)≥μ​f​(S)f(B)\geq\mu f(S) whenever S⊆BS\subseteq B. Every nonnegative function is 00-monotone, and 11-monotone functions are exactly the monotone ones.

Theorem 1.1 (Algorithm).

There is a randomized algorithm for the submodular secretary problem with a cardinality constraint that knows only nn and kk, accepts at most kk elements on every execution, makes at most 4​n+14n+1 value queries, each on a subset of the elements that have arrived, and satisfies the following, uniformly over n≥kn\geq k and ff.

  1. (a)

    If ff is nonnegative and submodular, then 𝔼⁡[f⁡(A)]≥(1/e−O⁡(log2⁡(k+1)/k))​OPT\mathbb{E}[f(A)]\geq\bigl(1/e-O(\log^{2}(k+1)/k)\bigr)\mathrm{OPT}.

  2. (b)

    If ff is nonnegative, monotone, and submodular, then 𝔼⁡[f⁡(A)]≥(1−1/e−O⁡(log⁡(k+1)/k))​OPT\mathbb{E}[f(A)]\geq\bigl(1-1/e-O(\log(k+1)/\sqrt{k})\bigr)\mathrm{OPT}.

  3. (c)

    More generally, if ff is μ\mu-monotone, then 𝔼⁡[f⁡(A)]≥(1/e+μ⁡(1−2/e)−O⁡(log⁡(k+1)/k))​OPT\mathbb{E}[f(A)]\geq\bigl(1/e+\mu(1-2/e)-O(\log(k+1)/\sqrt{k})\bigr)\mathrm{OPT}.

The same algorithm runs in all three cases and does not use μ\mu. The value-query model counts queries and treats real arithmetic as exact. Theorem 3.1 gives a bound with explicit constants.

For monotone objectives this is the best possible asymptotic ratio, even for computationally unbounded algorithms.

Theorem 1.2 (Hardness).

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be any randomized online algorithm, with unlimited computation and unlimited queries on subsets of arrived elements.

  1. (a)

    For every k≥2k\geq 2 and ε>0\varepsilon>0, there is a monotone coverage instance with budget kk on which 𝒜\mathcal{A} has ratio at most 1−(1−1/k)k+ε1-(1-1/k)^{k}+\varepsilon.

  2. (b)

    For every k≥64k\geq 64, there is a monotone coverage instance with budget kk and at most k2k^{2} elements on which 𝒜\mathcal{A} has ratio at most 1−1/e+O⁡(log⁡log⁡k/log⁡k)1-1/e+O(\log\log k/\log k).

Unlike the offline barrier of [NW78], Theorem 1.2 is information-theoretic, and it arises purely from the inability to see the future. Combining the two theorems pins down the problem.

Corollary 1.3 (Monotone objectives are settled).

Let ρkmon\rho^{\rm mon}_{k} be the optimal competitive ratio for the monotone submodular secretary problem with budget kk, over all algorithms with unlimited computation. Then limk→∞ρkmon=1−1/e\lim_{k\to\infty}\rho^{\rm mon}_{k}=1-1/e, and infk≥1ρkmon=ρ1mon=1/e\inf_{k\geq 1}\rho^{\rm mon}_{k}=\rho^{\rm mon}_{1}=1/e.

The limit follows from Theorems 1.1 and 1.2, and the worst case over budgets from Theorem B.1 (see Section 1.2), since the case k=1k=1 is the classical secretary problem. So both the asymptotic ratio and the ratio that can be guaranteed uniformly over all budgets are determined exactly. A shortlist is not needed to reach 1−1/e1-1/e, and unlimited computation does not help to exceed it.

For general objectives, 1/e1/e is not the limit.

Theorem 1.4 (Beyond 1/e1/e).

There is a randomized algorithm that knows only nn and kk, accepts at most kk elements, and makes polynomially many value queries on subsets of arrived elements, whose ratio on nonnegative submodular objectives is at least 1/e+3.5⋅10−61/e+3.5\cdot 10^{-6} for all sufficiently large kk, uniformly in nn.

The algorithm (Section 5) runs, with a small probability, a variant of Greedy restricted to a pool of promising elements, and otherwise a variant of AttenuatedPricing that measures its progress against two disjoint near-optimal sets at the start. Neither alone beats 1/e1/e on every instance, but their guarantees depend in opposite directions on one parameter of the instance, which neither of them computes.

In the other direction, there is a barrier strictly below 1−1/e1-1/e, which comes from nonmonotonicity.

Theorem 1.5 (General objectives).

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be any randomized online algorithm, with unlimited computation and unlimited queries on subsets of arrived elements.

  1. (a)

    For all n≥2n\geq 2, 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n, μ∈[0,1]\mu\in[0,1], and ε>0\varepsilon>0, there is a normalized μ\mu-monotone submodular instance on which 𝒜\mathcal{A} has ratio at most 1+μ2+ε\frac{1+\mu}{2}+\varepsilon. In particular, for general objectives the ratio is at most 12+ε\frac{1}{2}+\varepsilon.

  2. (b)

    For every sufficiently large kk, there is a normalized nonnegative submodular instance with budget kk on which 𝒜\mathcal{A} has ratio at most 0.4970530.497053, and in which every singleton has value at most 10−6​OPT10^{-6}\mathrm{OPT}. This holds even if 𝒜\mathcal{A} observes the arrival times.

Together with Theorem 1.4, this separates the general problem from both of its natural benchmarks.

Corollary 1.6 (General objectives).

Let ρk\rho_{k} be the optimal competitive ratio for nonnegative submodular objectives with budget kk, over all algorithms with unlimited computation. Then

1e<1e+3.5⋅10−6≤lim infk→∞ρk≤lim supk→∞ρk≤0.497053<12.\frac{1}{e}<\frac{1}{e}+3.5\cdot 10^{-6}\leq\liminf_{k\to\infty}\rho_{k}\leq\limsup_{k\to\infty}\rho_{k}\leq 0.497053<\frac{1}{2}.

So the limiting ratio for general objectives lies strictly between 1/e1/e and 1/21/2, and in particular strictly below the monotone limit 1−1/e1-1/e; the lower bound is achieved with polynomially many queries. Offline, unlimited queries solve the problem exactly, and so these barriers are purely a consequence of online decisions. For polynomial-query algorithms the offline bound of 0.4910.491 [OV11] is numerically stronger, but it has a different source, namely query complexity. The bound 12\frac{1}{2} in part (a) comes from pairs of elements that are valuable separately and worthless together, and part (b) goes below it with matroid gadgets (Section 7.2), which the pairs alone cannot do. For μ\mu-monotone objectives, since coverage functions are monotone, the upper bound is min⁡{1+μ2, 1−1/e}\min\{\frac{1+\mu}{2},\,1-1/e\} up to o⁡(1)o(1) terms, and the lower bound of Theorem 1.1(c) meets it only at μ=1\mu=1.

Table 1 summarizes the landscape.

1.2 Every budget

The guarantees of Theorems 1.1 and 1.4 take effect only for large kk. We also give explicit guarantees at every budget, with no error term, uniformly in n≥kn\geq k. For general objectives, some algorithm making at most 6​n+16n+1 value queries has ratio at least 0.26770.2677 for every kk; the ratio is at least 0.37340.3734 for k=2k=2, at least 0.30.3 for k≥52k\geq 52, and at least 0.36760.3676 for k≥106k\geq 10^{6} (Theorem A.1). It uses two picks for k≤3k\leq 3, for 4≤k≤294\leq k\leq 29 a multi-rank secretary rule that is restarted after every stop on a geometric time grid, and Poisson-tail prices with eligibility attenuation for larger kk. For monotone objectives, the ratio is at least 1/e1/e for every kk: exactly 1/e1/e for k=1k=1, more than 0.36960.3696 for every k≥2k\geq 2, and more than 12\frac{1}{2} for every k≥98k\geq 98 (Theorem B.1). It uses exact optimization over the observed prefix for k≤21k\leq 21, with O⁡(n21)O(n^{21}) queries, for 22≤k<10622\leq k<10^{6} a price policy mixed with the single-choice rule, with at most n+1n+1 queries, and for larger kk a variant of AttenuatedPricing. Since k=1k=1 contains the classical secretary problem, 1/e1/e cannot be improved as a bound that holds for all kk simultaneously. These results are proved in the appendices.

1.3 Technical overview

We describe the algorithm by building it up in three steps. Throughout, give each element an independent uniform arrival time in [0,1][0,1], and write f⁡(i∣A)=f⁡(A∪{i})−f⁡(A)f(i\mid A)=f(A\cup\{i\})-f(A).

Step 1: an idealized threshold rule.

Suppose the algorithm posts a price θt\theta_{t} and accepts an arrival ii exactly when f⁡(i∣At)>θtf(i\mid A_{t})>\theta_{t}, where AtA_{t} is the current accepted set. Let OO be an optimal set, F⁡(t)=𝔼​f​(At)F(t)=\mathbb{E}f(A_{t}), and zi​(t)=[f⁡(i∣At)−θt]+z_{i}(t)=\left[f(i\mid A_{t})-\theta_{t}\right]_{+} the score of ii. Each element of OO arrives in [t,t+d​t][t,t+dt] with probability d​tdt, and if accepted it gains its score plus the price. Suppose that we could charge every element of OO its current score at rate one. Submodularity gives ∑i∈Ozi​(t)≥f⁡(At∪O)−f⁡(At)−k​θt\sum_{i\in O}z_{i}(t)\geq f(A_{t}\cup O)-f(A_{t})-k\theta_{t}, and if ff is monotone, then f⁡(At∪O)≥OPTf(A_{t}\cup O)\geq\mathrm{OPT}. This yields F′≥OPT−F−k​𝔼​[θt]+(price revenue)F^{\prime}\geq\mathrm{OPT}-F-k\,\mathbb{E}[\theta_{t}]+(\text{price revenue}), and so F⁡(t)≥(1−e−t)​OPTF(t)\geq(1-e^{-t})\mathrm{OPT} as soon as the price revenue pays for the term k​𝔼​[θt]k\,\mathbb{E}[\theta_{t}].

The difficulty is that an element of OO produces its gain only once, at its arrival, while the inequality uses the score at time tt of every element of OO, including those that have already arrived, and against a state that these elements may have influenced. We relate the two with a deletion coupling: compare the run with the run in which ii is absent, and insert ii at a uniformly random time (Section 4.1).

Step 2: pacing without knowing the optimum.

For the price revenue to pay for k​𝔼​[θt]k\,\mathbb{E}[\theta_{t}], the rate of acceptances must track kk: acceptances should arrive at about rate kk whenever θt\theta_{t} is significant. We achieve this with an exponential price in the number of acceptances jj made so far, which falls at a controlled rate over time, of the form (up to a slowly varying factor)

θt≈M​exp⁡(λ⁡(j−b)−κ​t).\theta_{t}\;\approx\;M\exp\bigl(\lambda(j-b)-\kappa t\bigr).

A single unit of acceptance raises the price by a factor eλe^{\lambda}, and the time decay is calibrated so that the price is an exact potential: the revenue from acceptances equals k​∫θk\int\theta up to a boundary term (Lemma 4.4). Here MM is an estimate of the largest singleton value. It is what lets the algorithm work with no knowledge of OPT\mathrm{OPT}. An element whose singleton value exceeds MM is exceptional, and the algorithm raises MM and resets its price when such an element is accepted or has nonpositive marginal; there are only O⁡(log⁡k)O(\log k) such resets in expectation. A normal element has marginal at most MM, so once the price exceeds MM no normal element can be accepted, which gives a pathwise bound on the number of acceptances.

Step 3: eligibility attenuation.

For a general objective, the bound f⁡(At∪O)≥OPTf(A_{t}\cup O)\geq\mathrm{OPT} fails, and we must instead rely on the fact that f⁡(A∪O)f(A\cup O) is large in expectation whenever every element is unlikely to be in AA. In particular, if ℙ[i∈At]≤q\mathbb{P}[i\in A_{t}]\leq q for all ii, then 𝔼​f​(At∪O)≥(1−q)​OPT\mathbb{E}f(A_{t}\cup O)\geq(1-q)\mathrm{OPT}. Elementary thresholding only gives q≤tq\leq t, because an element arriving before tt might be accepted with certainty. To do better, we would like q=1−e−tq=1-e^{-t}, the same bound that drives the measured continuous greedy algorithm offline. However, simply discounting acceptances loses gain, and the loss seems unavoidable: an element accepted less often contributes less.

The solution is to discount each element according to its own history. Say ii is eligible at time ss if it would pass the price test against the state at time ss, and let τi​(t)\tau_{i}(t) be the total measure of times before tt at which it was eligible. We accept an eligible arrival at time tt with probability e−τi​(t)e^{-\tau_{i}(t)}. To see what this achieves, freeze the whole execution without ii, and insert ii at a uniformly random time. Before ii arrives, the execution is unaffected by it, so its eligibility function II is determined by the frozen execution, and

ℙ⁡[i​ accepted by time ​t]=∫0tI⁡(s)​e−τ⁡(s)​𝑑s=1−e−τ⁡(t).\mathbb{P}[i\text{ accepted by time }t]=\int_{0}^{t}I(s)\,e^{-\tau(s)}\,ds=1-e^{-\tau(t)}. (1)

This single identity has two consequences. Since τ⁡(t)≤t\tau(t)\leq t, every element is selected by time tt with probability at most 1−e−t1-e^{-t}, which gives the protection of f⁡(At∪O)f(A_{t}\cup O) that we wanted. And because e−τ⁡(t)e^{-\tau(t)} is exactly the probability that ii has not yet been selected, the attenuated rate of gain from ii arriving at time tt equals the expected residual score of ii at time tt, exactly matching the term needed in Step 1. Attenuation therefore costs nothing in the gain comparison. Solving the inequality F′+F≥e−t​OPT+⋯F^{\prime}+F\geq e^{-t}\mathrm{OPT}+\cdots gives t​e−t​OPTte^{-t}\mathrm{OPT}, which at t→1t\to 1 equals OPT/e\mathrm{OPT}/e, with zero first-order sensitivity at t=1t=1; this flatness is why the error term is as small as O⁡(log2⁡k/k)O(\log^{2}k/k). When ff is monotone, the very same execution has f⁡(At∪O)≥OPTf(A_{t}\cup O)\geq\mathrm{OPT} and yields 1−e−t1-e^{-t}.

Attenuation can be implemented with a linear number of queries in total, by checking historical eligibility only at the points of a rate-one Poisson process private to each element (Section 4.6).

Every budget.

For small budgets, prices are too coarse, since the accounting above loses lower-order terms that are large when kk is small. For k≤29k\leq 29 we instead select by rank, either of singleton values or of marginal values with a multi-rank rule that is restarted after every stop, and we bound the value by tracking how many elements of a fixed optimum are still unseen. For larger kk we use prices given by Poisson tail probabilities, which form an exact potential at every budget, together with eligibility attenuation (Appendix A). For monotone objectives at small kk, exact optimization over the observed prefix with a smaller sample than 1/e1/e suffices, and its guarantee reduces to a finite linear program (Appendix B).

Hardness.

The construction in Section 6 uses a coverage objective with sparse latent groups, adapted from the recent work of Udwani and Wajc on online welfare maximization [UW26]. Each element belongs to a group of rr types, and accepting all rr elements of a group has value one, while rr elements of distinct groups have value only about 1−1/e1-1/e. A random sparse subset of all types is present, chosen so that a complete group exists offline with high probability, but such that an element accepted online almost never has a future group mate. An online algorithm thus essentially always holds elements from distinct groups.

For general objectives, Section 7 uses a pair of elements a,ba,b that have values KJK^{J} and KJ+1K^{J+1} alone and value zero together, with JJ uniform over a long range. When the first of the two arrives with value vv, it is equally likely to be the light element, which should be rejected in favor of its partner, or the heavy one, which should be accepted, and no query can distinguish these cases until the partner arrives. Whichever decision is made is right about half of the time. Fixing the histogram of scales across many such pairs makes OPT\mathrm{OPT} a constant, removes any dominant element, and leaves this ambiguity in place at each pair. To go below 1/21/2, a small part of the value is moved into matroid gadgets: a matroid whose ground set is the union of a good basis GG and a bad basis BB, valued by r⁡(S)−|S∩B|r(S)-|S\cap B|, in which a random order lets bad elements displace good ones. A bad element that increases the rank of everything seen before it is invisible to every query at its arrival, and so it is rejected only as often as the algorithm rejects elements in general. The bad elements are carried by elements of lower levels of a hierarchy, at harmonically distributed distances, and a spectral estimate for the resulting circulant kernel turns these effects into a bound below 1/21/2 (Section 7.2).

Beyond 1/e1/e.

The analysis of AttenuatedPricing for general objectives compares the algorithm with a single optimal set. If two disjoint feasible sets have total value (1+d)​OPT(1+d)\mathrm{OPT}, then a variant that compares against both of them at the start gains Ω⁡(d)\Omega(d) over 1/e1/e. If dd is small, then every feasible set disjoint from an optimal set is worth at most d​OPTd\,\mathrm{OPT}, so the elements outside the optimum do little harm; a version of Greedy that trains on a sample, keeps only the arrivals with large marginal against the sample’s greedy solution, and paces its acceptances with prices, then obtains about 0.40.4, less a term linear in dd. The two guarantees depend on dd in opposite directions, and a fixed mixture beats 1/e1/e (Section 5).

1.4 Further related work

The submodular secretary problem has also been studied under matroid and other combinatorial constraints [BHZ13, GRST10, FZ18, KT17, Joy26]. Feldman and Zenklusen [FZ18] reduce matroid constraints with submodular objectives to the linear matroid secretary problem, and, together with the recent resolution of the matroid secretary conjecture [ABH+26], this yields a constant competitive ratio for every matroid. Agrawal, Shadravan, and Stein [ASS19], and later work [Sha20], study shortlists; [ASS19] also proves a 7/8+o⁡(1)7/8+o(1) upper bound that holds even with a shortlist, which is the previously best known information-theoretic upper bound for the cardinality case that we are aware of. Gupta et al. [GRST10] observed that no secretary algorithm can beat some universal constant, regardless of computation. In the related single-pass random-order streaming model, where an algorithm may keep and later discard elements in a memory buffer, Liu, Rubinstein, Vondrák, and Zhao [LRVZ21] obtain 1−1/e−ε1-1/e-\varepsilon for monotone and 1/e−ε1/e-\varepsilon for general objectives using O⁡(k/ε)O(k/\varepsilon) memory, and show that beating 1−1/e1-1/e requires Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) memory even with unlimited computation. Their lower bound depends on the memory limit, so it does not apply to secretary algorithms, which may remember every arrival but must decide immediately. Similarly, Rubinstein and Zhao [RZ22] show that no space-efficient random-order streaming algorithm can beat 1/21/2 for asymmetric objectives, while a ratio of 1/2+c1/2+c is possible for symmetric ones. Offline, Feige, Mirrokni, and Vondrák [FMV11] prove a 1/21/2 barrier for unconstrained maximization with polynomially many queries, a bound of the same value as our pairwise barrier but with a different source, namely query complexity. Theorem 1.1 shows that the limiting ratio 1−1/e1-1/e of the shortlist algorithm in [ASS19] can be achieved with no shortlist, and Theorem 1.2 improves this upper bound to 1−1/e+o⁡(1)1-1/e+o(1) when no shortlist is available.

Organization.

The body of the paper proves the main results. Section 2 sets up the model and a basic lemma. Section 3 presents the algorithm, Section 4 proves its guarantee and gives the linear-query implementation, which together prove Theorem 1.1. Section 5 goes beyond 1/e1/e for general objectives. Section 6 proves the hardness theorem for monotone objectives, and Section 7 proves the barrier 12\frac{1}{2} for general objectives and a bound strictly below it. The appendices contain the guarantees at every budget, for general objectives (Appendix A) and for monotone objectives (Appendix B), and the proof of the constant 0.4970530.497053 (Appendix C).

2 Preliminaries

Model and notation.

The ground set is EE, with |E|=n≥k≥1|E|=n\geq k\geq 1. The function f:2E→ℝ≥0f:2^{E}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} is submodular: f⁡(e∣A)≥f⁡(e∣B)f(e\mid A)\geq f(e\mid B) whenever A⊆BA\subseteq B and e∉Be\notin B, where f⁡(e∣A)=f⁡(A∪{e})−f⁡(A)f(e\mid A)=f(A\cup\{e\})-f(A). It is not assumed to be normalized. Write OPT=max|S|≤k⁡f⁡(S)\mathrm{OPT}=\max_{|S|\leq k}f(S). All logarithms are natural.

Timestamps.

It is standard to generate a uniform random order from timestamps. The algorithm draws nn independent uniforms on [0,1][0,1], sorts them, and assigns the jjth smallest to the jjth arrival. Because the arrival order is uniform and independent of these numbers, the timestamps of the fixed elements of EE are independent uniforms. Timestamps are almost surely distinct, and we assume this from now on. The algorithm uses the timestamps only of elements that have already arrived.

The following lemma is a form of a well-known sampling bound [FMV11, BFNS14]. We include the proof because we need the dependence on μ\mu.

Lemma 2.1 (Random sets).

Let g:2E→ℝ≥0g:2^{E}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be submodular and let μ∈[0,1]\mu\in[0,1] satisfy g⁡(X)≥μ​g​(∅)g(X)\geq\mu\,g(\emptyset) for all XX. If SS is a random subset of EE, with arbitrary correlations, and ℙ[e∈S]≤q\mathbb{P}[e\in S]\leq q for each ee, then

𝔼⁡[g⁡(S)]≥(1−(1−μ)​q)​g​(∅).\mathbb{E}[g(S)]\geq\bigl(1-(1-\mu)q\bigr)\,g(\emptyset).
Proof.

Order E={e1,…,eN}E=\{e_{1},\dots,e_{N}\} by nonincreasing inclusion probabilities q1≥⋯≥qNq_{1}\geq\dots\geq q_{N}, and let Si={e1,…,ei}S_{i}=\{e_{1},\dots,e_{i}\}. Adding the elements of SS in this order and using submodularity gives g(S)≥g(∅)+∑i:ei∈S(g(Si)−g(Si−1))g(S)\geq g(\emptyset)+\sum_{i:\,e_{i}\in S}(g(S_{i})-g(S_{i-1})). Taking expectations and summing by parts yields

𝔼⁡[g⁡(S)]≥(1−q1)​g​(∅)+∑i=1N−1(qi−qi+1)​g​(Si)+qN​g​(SN).\mathbb{E}[g(S)]\geq(1-q_{1})\,g(\emptyset)+\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}(q_{i}-q_{i+1})\,g(S_{i})+q_{N}\,g(S_{N}). (2)

All coefficients are nonnegative and those of the sets S1,…,SNS_{1},\dots,S_{N} sum to q1q_{1}. Each such set has value at least μ​g​(∅)\mu\,g(\emptyset), so 𝔼⁡[g⁡(S)]≥(1−(1−μ)​q1)​g​(∅)≥(1−(1−μ)​q)​g​(∅)\mathbb{E}[g(S)]\geq(1-(1-\mu)q_{1})\,g(\emptyset)\geq(1-(1-\mu)q)\,g(\emptyset). ∎

3 The algorithm

Fix kk large enough that the horizon TT below is positive; for smaller kk the algorithm returns ∅\emptyset, and Theorem 1.1 holds vacuously after enlarging the hidden constants. Define

L=ln⁡(k+1),p=1k,b=⌈k⌉,λ=4​Lb,m=⌈200​L⌉,\displaystyle L=\ln(k+1),\quad p=\frac{1}{k},\quad b=\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil,\quad\lambda=\frac{4L}{b},\quad m=\lceil 200L\rceil,
ν=eλ−1λ,κ=k⁡(eλ−1),T=k−(m+1)​(b+1)−mν​k,h⁡(t)=et−T.\displaystyle\nu=\frac{e^{\lambda}-1}{\lambda},\quad\kappa=k(e^{\lambda}-1),\quad T=\frac{k-(m+1)(b+1)-m}{\nu k},\quad h(t)=e^{t-T}.

Note that T<1T<1 and h≤1h\leq 1 on [0,T][0,T].

AttenuatedPricing. Each element ii has an independent uniform timestamp and an independent private uniform Ui∈[0,1]U_{i}\in[0,1].

  1. 1.

    Sample. Reject every element with timestamp below pp. Let MM be the largest singleton value f⁡({e})f(\{e\}) among them, or 00 if there are none. Rescale the remaining time to t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], via t=(timestamp−p)/(1−p)t=(\text{timestamp}-p)/(1-p). Reject all arrivals after time TT.

  2. 2.

    State and price. Maintain the accepted set AA, the scale MM, the epoch start ss (initially 00), and the epoch count jj (initially 00). At time tt, the price is

    θt=1h⁡(t)​M​exp⁡(λ⁡(j−b)−κ⁡(t−s)).\theta_{t}=\frac{1}{h(t)}\,M\exp\bigl(\lambda(j-b)-\kappa(t-s)\bigr).
  3. 3.

    Eligibility. Element ii is exceptional at time uu if f⁡({i})>Muf(\{i\})>M_{u}, and otherwise normal, where MuM_{u} is the scale just before time uu. With w=f⁡(i∣Au)w=f(i\mid A_{u}) the marginal against the accepted set just before uu, an exceptional element is eligible at uu if w>0w>0, and a normal element is eligible at uu if w>θuw>\theta_{u}. Let Ii​(u)∈{0,1}I_{i}(u)\in\{0,1\} indicate eligibility, a counterfactual test that makes sense even for times uu before ii arrives, and let τi​(t)=∫0tIi​(u)​𝑑u\tau_{i}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}I_{i}(u)\,du.

  4. 4.

    Decision. When ii arrives at time tt, accept it if and only if Ii​(t)=1I_{i}(t)=1 and Ui≤e−τi​(t)U_{i}\leq e^{-\tau_{i}(t)}.

  5. 5.

    Update. If ii is normal and accepted, set j←j+1j\leftarrow j+1. If ii is exceptional and either accepted or has w≤0w\leq 0, then start a new epoch: set M←f⁡({i})M\leftarrow f(\{i\}), s←ts\leftarrow t, and j←0j\leftarrow 0. No other arrival changes the state.

  6. 6.

    Budget. Once kk elements are accepted, reject everything.

Eligibility at an earlier time uu concerns the element ii at hand together with the state that actually existed at time uu, so all queries are on arrived elements. (The state consists of AuA_{u}, which is a subset of the arrived elements, and three numbers.) Between state changes, θu\theta_{u} is nonincreasing in uu, since h⁡(u)h(u) grows and the exponential falls. Hence each IiI_{i} is piecewise constant with finitely many pieces and the integral τi\tau_{i} is well defined and measurable. An exceptional element with positive marginal that fails its test in step 4 leaves the state unchanged. This is important for the analysis, since a state change caused by a rejected element is harmful in general; the only rejected elements that change the state have nonpositive marginal.

The uncapped execution.

In the analysis we also consider the uncapped execution, which is identical except that step 6 is omitted. Let BB be its number of acceptances and DD its number of epoch resets. Both executions agree until the capped one makes its kkth acceptance.

Theorem 3.1 (Finite guarantee).

Let ff be nonnegative, submodular, and μ\mu-monotone, and suppose T>0T>0. Then AttenuatedPricing accepts at most kk elements on every execution, and

𝔼⁡[f⁡(A)]≥[(1−p)​Λμ​(T)−200(k+1)3]​OPT,whereΛμ​(T)=μ⁡(1−e−T)+(1−μ)​T​e−T.\mathbb{E}[f(A)]\geq\Bigl[(1-p)\Lambda_{\mu}(T)-\frac{200}{(k+1)^{3}}\Bigr]\mathrm{OPT},\qquad\text{where}\quad\Lambda_{\mu}(T)=\mu\bigl(1-e^{-T}\bigr)+(1-\mu)\,T\,e^{-T}.
Remark 3.2.

The constants in Section 3 are chosen for a simple proof. In particular, T>0T>0 requires kk of order 10710^{7}. Appendices A and B give explicit guarantees at every budget, for general and for monotone objectives.

Proof of Theorem 1.1 from Theorems 3.1 and 4.7.

We have (m+1)​(b+1)+m=O⁡(L​k)(m+1)(b+1)+m=O(L\sqrt{k}) and λ=O⁡(L/k)\lambda=O(L/\sqrt{k}), and ν≤1+λ\nu\leq 1+\lambda for λ≤1\lambda\leq 1. It follows that T>0T>0 for large kk and that δ:=1−T=O⁡(L/k)\delta:=1-T=O(L/\sqrt{k}). Since x↦x​e−xx\mapsto xe^{-x} has derivative zero at x=1x=1 and second derivative at most 22 in absolute value on [0,1][0,1], we get T​e−T≥1/e−δ2Te^{-T}\geq 1/e-\delta^{2}. Also 1−e−T≥1−1/e−δ1-e^{-T}\geq 1-1/e-\delta. For μ=0\mu=0 this gives (a), since δ2=O⁡(L2/k)\delta^{2}=O(L^{2}/k) and p=1/kp=1/k. For general μ\mu we have Λμ​(T)≥1/e+μ⁡(1−2/e)−δ\Lambda_{\mu}(T)\geq 1/e+\mu(1-2/e)-\delta, proving (b) and (c). Proposition 4.7 gives the query bound and adds an error of e−Ω⁡(k)e^{-\Omega(k)}, which is absorbed in the error terms. ∎

4 Analysis

Section 4.1 compares an execution with the execution where one element is removed, and Section 4.2 deduces a lower bound on the value. This bound contains a term for prices, which we pay for in Section 4.3. Finally, Section 4.4 bounds the number of resets, Section 4.5 completes the proof, and Section 4.6 gives the linear-query implementation.

Throughout Sections 4.1 and 4.2, we analyze the uncapped execution conditional on the set S0S_{0} of sampled elements. Thus M0M_{0}, the initial scale, is fixed, and the remaining elements R=E∖S0R=E\setminus S_{0} have independent uniform rescaled timestamps ti∈[0,1]t_{i}\in[0,1]. Let 𝔼0\mathbb{E}_{0} and ℙ0\mathbb{P}_{0} denote the conditional expectation and probability. For a time tt, let Xt=(At,Mt,st,jt)X_{t}=(A_{t},M_{t},s_{t},j_{t}) denote the state just before time tt. For any element ii, define the score

zi​(t)=[f⁡(i∣At)−θt]+.z_{i}(t)=\left[f(i\mid A_{t})-\theta_{t}\right]_{+}.

4.1 The deletion coupling

Fix i∈Ri\in R, and fix all the randomness ωi=(tj,Uj)j∈R∖{i}\omega_{i}=(t_{j},U_{j})_{j\in R\setminus\{i\}} other than (ti,Ui)(t_{i},U_{i}). The deleted run is the uncapped execution on R∖{i}R\setminus\{i\} with the same randomness and parameters. We add a superscript “−-” to its quantities: Xt−X_{t}^{-}, θt−\theta_{t}^{-}, and zi−​(t)z_{i}^{-}(t), as well as Ii−​(t)I_{i}^{-}(t) and τi−​(t)\tau_{i}^{-}(t), which test the (absent) element ii against the state Xt−X_{t}^{-}. All of these are functions of ωi\omega_{i} only.

Lemma 4.1 (Deletion identities).

Fix i∈Ri\in R, ωi\omega_{i}, and t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], and let ℰi​(t)\mathcal{E}_{i}(t) be the event that ii has been accepted before time tt. Conditional on ωi\omega_{i}:

  1. (a)

    If ti=ut_{i}=u, then ii is eligible at its arrival if and only if Ii−​(u)=1I_{i}^{-}(u)=1, and it passes step 4 if and only if Ui≤e−τi−​(u)U_{i}\leq e^{-\tau_{i}^{-}(u)}.

  2. (b)

    ℙ⁡[ℰi​(t)∣ωi]=1−e−τi−​(t)≤1−e−t\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{i}(t)\mid\omega_{i}]=1-e^{-\tau_{i}^{-}(t)}\leq 1-e^{-t}.

  3. (c)

    zi​(t)=0z_{i}(t)=0 on ℰi​(t)\mathcal{E}_{i}(t), and zi​(t)=zi−​(t)z_{i}(t)=z_{i}^{-}(t) outside ℰi​(t)\mathcal{E}_{i}(t). Hence 𝔼⁡[zi​(t)∣ωi]=e−τi−​(t)​zi−​(t)\mathbb{E}[z_{i}(t)\mid\omega_{i}]=e^{-\tau_{i}^{-}(t)}\,z_{i}^{-}(t).

Proof.

(a) Before time tit_{i} the two runs process the same arrivals with the same decisions, by induction over arrivals: an element’s decision depends only on the earlier state history. Therefore Xv=Xv−X_{v}=X_{v}^{-} for all v≤tiv\leq t_{i}, which implies Ii​(v)=Ii−​(v)I_{i}(v)=I_{i}^{-}(v) for such vv and so τi​(ti)=τi−​(ti)\tau_{i}(t_{i})=\tau_{i}^{-}(t_{i}).

(b) By (a), ℰi​(t)\mathcal{E}_{i}(t) occurs if and only if ti<tt_{i}<t, Ii−​(ti)=1I_{i}^{-}(t_{i})=1, and Ui≤e−τi−​(ti)U_{i}\leq e^{-\tau_{i}^{-}(t_{i})}. Since tit_{i} and UiU_{i} are independent uniforms independent of ωi\omega_{i}, and τi−\tau_{i}^{-} is absolutely continuous with derivative Ii−I_{i}^{-} almost everywhere,

ℙ⁡[ℰi​(t)∣ωi]=∫0tIi−​(u)​e−τi−​(u)​𝑑u=1−e−τi−​(t).\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{i}(t)\mid\omega_{i}]=\int_{0}^{t}I_{i}^{-}(u)\,e^{-\tau_{i}^{-}(u)}\,du=1-e^{-\tau_{i}^{-}(t)}.

The inequality uses τi−​(t)≤t\tau_{i}^{-}(t)\leq t.

(c) If i∈Ati\in A_{t} then f⁡(i∣At)=0f(i\mid A_{t})=0 and, as θt≥0\theta_{t}\geq 0, the score vanishes. Suppose ii is not accepted before tt. If ti≥tt_{i}\geq t, then Xt=Xt−X_{t}=X_{t}^{-} by (a) and the two scores agree. If ti<tt_{i}<t and the rejection of ii did not change the state, then the two runs continue identically, and again Xt=Xt−X_{t}=X_{t}^{-}. The only remaining case is a rejection of ii that started a new epoch. In that case ii had marginal at most zero at tit_{i} against Ati=Ati−A_{t_{i}}=A_{t_{i}}^{-}. The accepted sets At⊇AtiA_{t}\supseteq A_{t_{i}} and At−⊇Ati−A_{t}^{-}\supseteq A_{t_{i}}^{-} only grow, so by submodularity f⁡(i∣At)≤0f(i\mid A_{t})\leq 0 and f⁡(i∣At−)≤0f(i\mid A_{t}^{-})\leq 0, whence zi​(t)=zi−​(t)=0z_{i}(t)=z_{i}^{-}(t)=0. Combining this with (b) proves the formula for the conditional expectation. ∎

Lemma 4.1(b) also gives the inclusion bound ℙ0[i∈At]≤1−e−t\mathbb{P}_{0}[i\in A_{t}]\leq 1-e^{-t} for each i∈Ri\in R. Elements outside RR are never accepted.

4.2 The value inequality

Let NN be the counting process of normal acceptances. For an arrival ii at time ti≤Tt_{i}\leq T, let gaini\mathrm{gain}_{i} be the increase in f⁡(A)f(A) that it causes, which is positive if ii is accepted and zero otherwise, and define its net gain

neti=gaini−θti​𝟏​[i​ is accepted as a normal element].\mathrm{net}_{i}=\mathrm{gain}_{i}-\theta_{t_{i}}\mathbf{1}[i\text{ is accepted as a normal element}].

Net gains are nonnegative, because normal acceptance requires a marginal larger than θti\theta_{t_{i}}.

Lemma 4.2.

Let O⊆RO\subseteq R be a fixed set. For every measurable ψ:[0,T]→ℝ≥0\psi:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0},

𝔼0[∑i∈R:ti≤Tψ(ti)neti]≥∫0Tψ(t)𝔼0[∑i∈Ozi(t)]dt.\mathbb{E}_{0}\Bigl[\sum_{i\in R:\,t_{i}\leq T}\psi(t_{i})\,\mathrm{net}_{i}\Bigr]\geq\int_{0}^{T}\psi(t)\,\mathbb{E}_{0}\Bigl[\sum_{i\in O}z_{i}(t)\Bigr]\,dt.
Proof.

Discard the nonnegative terms with i∉Oi\notin O. For i∈Oi\in O, condition on ωi\omega_{i} and on ti=tt_{i}=t. By Lemma 4.1(a), element ii meets the state Xt−X^{-}_{t} upon arrival. If it is a normal element then it is accepted with probability Ii−​(t)​e−τi−​(t)I_{i}^{-}(t)e^{-\tau_{i}^{-}(t)}, and in this case neti=zi−​(t)\mathrm{net}_{i}=z_{i}^{-}(t); as zi−​(t)>0z_{i}^{-}(t)>0 implies eligibility, 𝔼[neti∣ωi,ti=t]=e−τi−​(t)zi−(t)\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{net}_{i}\mid\omega_{i},t_{i}=t]=e^{-\tau_{i}^{-}(t)}z_{i}^{-}(t). If it is exceptional and eligible, then 𝔼[neti∣ωi,ti=t]=e−τi−​(t)f(i∣At−)≥e−τi−​(t)zi−(t)\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{net}_{i}\mid\omega_{i},t_{i}=t]=e^{-\tau_{i}^{-}(t)}f(i\mid A_{t}^{-})\geq e^{-\tau_{i}^{-}(t)}z_{i}^{-}(t). If it is exceptional and ineligible, its marginal is nonpositive and both sides vanish. In every case, by Lemma 4.1(c),

𝔼[neti∣ωi,ti=t]≥e−τi−​(t)zi−(t)=𝔼[zi(t)∣ωi].\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{net}_{i}\mid\omega_{i},t_{i}=t]\geq e^{-\tau_{i}^{-}(t)}z_{i}^{-}(t)=\mathbb{E}[z_{i}(t)\mid\omega_{i}].

Integrating over tit_{i}, which has density 11, and then over ωi\omega_{i} proves the claim. ∎

We can now derive the main inequality. Note how the integrating factor removes all dependence on the unknown process f⁡(At)f(A_{t}). Recall that h⁡(t)=et−Th(t)=e^{t-T}, so h′=hh^{\prime}=h and h⁡(T)=1h(T)=1.

Lemma 4.3 (Value inequality).

Let O⊆RO\subseteq R with |O|≤k|O|\leq k. If ff is μ\mu-monotone, then the uncapped execution satisfies

𝔼0​[f⁡(AT)]≥Λμ​(T)​f​(O)+𝔼0​[∫0Th⁡(t)​θt​𝑑N​(t)−k​∫0Th⁡(t)​θt​𝑑t].\mathbb{E}_{0}[f(A_{T})]\geq\Lambda_{\mu}(T)\,f(O)+\mathbb{E}_{0}\Bigl[\int_{0}^{T}h(t)\theta_{t}\,dN(t)-k\int_{0}^{T}h(t)\theta_{t}\,dt\Bigr].
Proof.

Since f⁡(At)f(A_{t}) is piecewise constant, integrating by parts gives

∑i:ti≤Th(ti)gaini=f(AT)−h(0)f(∅)−∫0Th(t)f(At)dt.\sum_{i:\,t_{i}\leq T}h(t_{i})\,\mathrm{gain}_{i}=f(A_{T})-h(0)f(\emptyset)-\int_{0}^{T}h(t)f(A_{t})\,dt.

Apply Lemma 4.2 with ψ=h\psi=h and write π⁡(t)=𝔼0​[θt]\pi(t)=\mathbb{E}_{0}[\theta_{t}]. The left side of Lemma 4.2 equals the expectation of the display minus 𝔼0​∫h​θ​𝑑N\mathbb{E}_{0}\int h\theta\,dN. For the right side, submodularity and θt≥0\theta_{t}\geq 0 give, pointwise,

∑i∈Ozi​(t)≥∑i∈Of⁡(i∣At)−k​θt≥f⁡(At∪O)−f⁡(At)−k​θt.\sum_{i\in O}z_{i}(t)\geq\sum_{i\in O}f(i\mid A_{t})-k\theta_{t}\geq f(A_{t}\cup O)-f(A_{t})-k\theta_{t}.

Substituting and cancelling ∫h​𝔼0​f​(At)​𝑑t\int h\,\mathbb{E}_{0}f(A_{t})\,dt from both sides, and dropping the nonnegative term h⁡(0)​f​(∅)h(0)f(\emptyset), we obtain

𝔼0​[f⁡(AT)]≥∫0Th⁡(t)​𝔼0​[f⁡(At∪O)]​𝑑t+𝔼0​∫0Th​θ​𝑑N−k​∫0Th⁡(t)​π​(t)​𝑑t.\mathbb{E}_{0}[f(A_{T})]\geq\int_{0}^{T}h(t)\,\mathbb{E}_{0}[f(A_{t}\cup O)]\,dt+\mathbb{E}_{0}\int_{0}^{T}h\theta\,dN-k\int_{0}^{T}h(t)\pi(t)\,dt.

The function g⁡(S)=f⁡(O∪S)g(S)=f(O\cup S) is nonnegative and submodular, with g⁡(∅)=f⁡(O)g(\emptyset)=f(O), and μ\mu-monotonicity of ff gives g⁡(X)≥μ​g​(∅)g(X)\geq\mu\,g(\emptyset). By Lemma 2.1 with q=1−e−tq=1-e^{-t} and the inclusion bound,

𝔼0​[f⁡(At∪O)]≥(1−(1−μ)​(1−e−t))​f​(O)=(μ+(1−μ)​e−t)​f​(O).\mathbb{E}_{0}[f(A_{t}\cup O)]\geq\bigl(1-(1-\mu)(1-e^{-t})\bigr)f(O)=\bigl(\mu+(1-\mu)e^{-t}\bigr)f(O).

Finally ∫0Tet−T​(μ+(1−μ)​e−t)​𝑑t=μ⁡(1−e−T)+(1−μ)​T​e−T=Λμ​(T)\int_{0}^{T}e^{t-T}\bigl(\mu+(1-\mu)e^{-t}\bigr)\,dt=\mu(1-e^{-T})+(1-\mu)Te^{-T}=\Lambda_{\mu}(T). ∎

4.3 Paying for prices and bounding acceptances

The next lemma holds on every sample path of the uncapped execution.

Lemma 4.4 (Prices and counts).

On every execution, Mt≤OPTM_{t}\leq\mathrm{OPT} for all tt, and:

  1. (a)

    ∫0Th​θ​𝑑N−k​∫0Th​θ​𝑑t≥−(D+1)​e−λ​beλ−1​OPT\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}h\theta\,dN-k\int_{0}^{T}h\theta\,dt\ \geq\ -(D+1)\,\frac{e^{-\lambda b}}{e^{\lambda}-1}\,\mathrm{OPT};

  2. (b)

    B≤k+(b+2)​(D−m)B\leq k+(b+2)(D-m).

Proof.

The scale is either zero or a singleton value, so Mt≤OPTM_{t}\leq\mathrm{OPT}. Write ψt=h⁡(t)​θt=M​exp⁡(λ⁡(j−b)−κ⁡(t−s))\psi_{t}=h(t)\theta_{t}=M\exp(\lambda(j-b)-\kappa(t-s)) and Ψt=ψt/(eλ−1)\Psi_{t}=\psi_{t}/(e^{\lambda}-1).

(a) Within one epoch, Ψ\Psi decreases continuously at rate κ​Ψ=k​ψ\kappa\Psi=k\psi, and a normal acceptance multiplies Ψ\Psi by eλe^{\lambda}, raising it by exactly (eλ−1)​Ψ=ψ(e^{\lambda}-1)\Psi=\psi. Thus over one epoch, Ψend−Ψstart\Psi_{\mathrm{end}}-\Psi_{\mathrm{start}} equals the contribution of that epoch to ∫ψ​𝑑N−k​∫ψ​𝑑t\int\psi\,dN-k\int\psi\,dt. As Ψend≥0\Psi_{\mathrm{end}}\geq 0 and Ψstart=M​e−λ​b/(eλ−1)≤OPT​e−λ​b/(eλ−1)\Psi_{\mathrm{start}}=Me^{-\lambda b}/(e^{\lambda}-1)\leq\mathrm{OPT}e^{-\lambda b}/(e^{\lambda}-1), summing over the D+1D+1 epochs gives (a).

(b) A normal element ii has f⁡(i∣A)≤f⁡({i})−f⁡(∅)≤Mf(i\mid A)\leq f(\{i\})-f(\emptyset)\leq M. Normal acceptance therefore forces θt<M\theta_{t}<M, and in particular M>0M>0. Since h≤1h\leq 1, this gives ψt≤θt<M\psi_{t}\leq\theta_{t}<M, hence λ⁡(j−b)<κ⁡(t−s)\lambda(j-b)<\kappa(t-s), that is, j<b+ν​k​(t−s)j<b+\nu k(t-s), using κ/λ=ν​k\kappa/\lambda=\nu k. Thus an epoch of length ℓ\ell contains at most ν​k​ℓ+b+1\nu k\ell+b+1 normal acceptances. Summing over the D+1D+1 epochs and adding at most DD exceptional acceptances, each of which starts an epoch,

B\displaystyle B ≤ν​k​T+(D+1)​(b+1)+D\displaystyle\leq\nu kT+(D+1)(b+1)+D
=k−(m+1)​(b+1)−m+(D+1)​(b+1)+D=k+(b+2)​(D−m).∎\displaystyle=k-(m+1)(b+1)-m+(D+1)(b+1)+D=k+(b+2)(D-m).\qed

4.4 The number of resets

Attenuation makes the reset count subtle: a large element that fails its test does not update the scale, so resets are not dominated by ordinary records. The following argument gets around this.

Lemma 4.5 (Tail bound).

For every integer j≥1j\geq 1, ℙ[D≥j]≤e−j/(8e)+k 2−j/(2e)\mathbb{P}[D\geq j]\leq e^{-j/(8e)}+k\,2^{-j/(2e)}. Consequently 𝔼⁡[(D−m)+]≤32​(k+1)−9\mathbb{E}[(D-m)_{+}]\leq 32(k+1)^{-9} and 𝔼⁡[D]≤m+32\mathbb{E}[D]\leq m+32.

Proof.

Work on the original time scale, and fix a tie-breaking order on singleton values so that all elements have distinct ranks. Say an element is marked if Ui≤1/eU_{i}\leq 1/e; include sampled elements, for which UiU_{i} is otherwise unused. Marks are independent of timestamps, and each element is marked with probability q=1/eq=1/e.

A marked eligible element always passes step 4, because τi​(t)≤t≤1\tau_{i}(t)\leq t\leq 1. It follows by induction that at every moment MM is at least the singleton value of every marked element that has arrived. This is true for the sample, and a marked arrival whose singleton value exceeds MM is exceptional: it is accepted if it has positive marginal, and it starts a new epoch either way. So MM rises to its singleton value.

Call a post-sample arrival a candidate if its rank beats that of every earlier marked element, whether or not we have stopped, and let CC be the number of candidates in the stream. A reset element has singleton value strictly above MM, so it is a candidate, and D≤CD\leq C.

Whether an arrival is a candidate is determined by the timestamps and by the marks of earlier elements. Therefore, revealing elements in order of arrival, the marks of successive candidates are independent Bernoulli(q)(q) variables. (Pad the sequence with fresh draws, if needed.) Let R′R^{\prime} be the number of marked candidates. If C≥jC\geq j, then either fewer than q​j/2qj/2 of the first jj candidates are marked, which has probability at most e−qj/8e^{-qj/8} by the Chernoff bound, or R′≥q​j/2R^{\prime}\geq qj/2.

Marked candidates are exactly the records after time pp in the subsequence of marked elements. Condition on there being ℓ\ell marked elements. Their relative order is a uniform permutation, independent of the number S∼Bin⁡(ℓ,p)S\sim\mathrm{Bin}(\ell,p) of them in the sample. So the record indicators are independent, with the xxth position being a record with probability 1/x1/x, and

𝔼[2R′∣ℓ,S]=∏x=S+1ℓ(1+1x)=ℓ+1S+1,𝔼[2R′∣ℓ]=1−(1−p)ℓ+1p≤1p=k.\mathbb{E}[2^{R^{\prime}}\mid\ell,S]=\prod_{x=S+1}^{\ell}\Bigl(1+\frac{1}{x}\Bigr)=\frac{\ell+1}{S+1},\qquad\mathbb{E}[2^{R^{\prime}}\mid\ell]=\frac{1-(1-p)^{\ell+1}}{p}\leq\frac{1}{p}=k.

By Markov’s inequality ℙ[R′≥qj/2]≤k 2−qj/2\mathbb{P}[R^{\prime}\geq qj/2]\leq k\,2^{-qj/2}, proving the tail bound.

For the consequences, 𝔼[(D−m)+]=∑j>mℙ[D≥j]\mathbb{E}[(D-m)_{+}]=\sum_{j>m}\mathbb{P}[D\geq j]. Let x=e−1/(8e)x=e^{-1/(8e)} and y=2−1/(2e)y=2^{-1/(2e)}, so that 1/(1−x)≤231/(1-x)\leq 23, 1/(1−y)≤91/(1-y)\leq 9, and, using m≥200​Lm\geq 200L, we have xm≤(k+1)−9x^{m}\leq(k+1)^{-9} and ym≤(k+1)−25y^{m}\leq(k+1)^{-25}. Summing the geometric series gives 𝔼⁡[(D−m)+]≤23​(k+1)−9+9​k​(k+1)−25≤32​(k+1)−9\mathbb{E}[(D-m)_{+}]\leq 23(k+1)^{-9}+9k(k+1)^{-25}\leq 32(k+1)^{-9}. Finally, 𝔼⁡[D]≤m+𝔼⁡[(D−m)+]\mathbb{E}[D]\leq m+\mathbb{E}[(D-m)_{+}]. ∎

4.5 Completing the proof of Theorem 3.1

The accepted set has size at most kk by construction. Let O∗O^{*} be an optimal set and let O=O∗∖S0O=O^{*}\setminus S_{0}, which is a feasible subset of RR. Taking expectations over the sample in Lemma 4.3 and applying Lemma 4.4(a) gives, for the uncapped set ATA_{T},

𝔼⁡[f⁡(AT)]≥Λμ​(T)​𝔼​[f⁡(O∗∖S0)]−(𝔼⁡[D]+1)​e−λ​beλ−1​OPT.\mathbb{E}[f(A_{T})]\geq\Lambda_{\mu}(T)\,\mathbb{E}[f(O^{*}\setminus S_{0})]-(\mathbb{E}[D]+1)\,\frac{e^{-\lambda b}}{e^{\lambda}-1}\,\mathrm{OPT}.

Lemma 2.1, applied to g⁡(S)=f⁡(O∗∖S)g(S)=f(O^{*}\setminus S) with μ=0\mu=0 and q=pq=p, gives 𝔼⁡[f⁡(O∗∖S0)]≥(1−p)​OPT\mathbb{E}[f(O^{*}\setminus S_{0})]\geq(1-p)\mathrm{OPT}.

Now let AA be the output. The capped execution matches the uncapped one up to the capped execution’s kkth acceptance, so A⊆ATA\subseteq A_{T} and f⁡(AT)−f⁡(A)f(A_{T})-f(A) is a sum of at most (B−k)+(B-k)_{+} gains. Each gain is at most the singleton value of the element, and thus at most OPT\mathrm{OPT}. By Lemma 4.4(b), 𝔼⁡[f⁡(AT)]−𝔼⁡[f⁡(A)]≤(b+2)​𝔼​[(D−m)+]​OPT\mathbb{E}[f(A_{T})]-\mathbb{E}[f(A)]\leq(b+2)\mathbb{E}[(D-m)_{+}]\,\mathrm{OPT}.

It remains to bound the errors. Since λ​b=4​L\lambda b=4L and eλ−1≥λ=4​L/be^{\lambda}-1\geq\lambda=4L/b, we get

(𝔼⁡[D]+1)​e−λ​beλ−1≤(200​L+34)​b4​L​(k+1)4≤63​(k+1)−3,(\mathbb{E}[D]+1)\,\frac{e^{-\lambda b}}{e^{\lambda}-1}\leq\frac{(200L+34)\,b}{4L\,(k+1)^{4}}\leq 63\,(k+1)^{-3},

using L≥ln⁡2L\geq\ln 2 and b≤k+1b\leq k+1. Also (b+2)​𝔼​[(D−m)+]≤3​(k+1)⋅32​(k+1)−9≤96​(k+1)−8(b+2)\mathbb{E}[(D-m)_{+}]\leq 3(k+1)\cdot 32(k+1)^{-9}\leq 96(k+1)^{-8}. Together these are at most 200​(k+1)−3200(k+1)^{-3}, completing the proof. ∎

Remark 4.6.

Two features of the proof deserve mention. First, nothing is lost in the price accounting to first order, because the exponential potential of Lemma 4.4 is exact. Apart from the factor 1−p1-p and lower-order reset terms, the error comes from T<1T<1, and when μ=0\mu=0 that error is second-order. Second, the monotone case is not a separate analysis: the only property used in the proof is g⁡(X)≥μ​g​(∅)g(X)\geq\mu\,g(\emptyset) in Lemma 4.3. For monotone objectives, attenuation is unnecessary (Section B.3).

4.6 Linear query complexity

As described in Section 3, the algorithm computes τi​(t)\tau_{i}(t) exactly. Since the accepted set takes at most k+1k+1 distinct values, and eligibility on an interval where the accepted set is fixed requires only its one marginal value, this takes O⁡(n​k)O(nk) value queries in total. We can instead use a randomized test with the same acceptance probability, as follows.

Give each element ii a private rate-one Poisson process PiP_{i} on [0,1][0,1]. When ii arrives at time tt and is eligible, accept it if and only if no point u∈Pi∩[0,t)u\in P_{i}\cap[0,t) has Ii​(u)=1I_{i}(u)=1. The algorithm stores the accepted elements in order, together with their acceptance times, the cached values f⁡(Au)f(A_{u}), and the history of scales and epochs, so a test at uu costs one query, namely f⁡(Au∪{i})f(A_{u}\cup\{i\}). Finally, stop the algorithm permanently before it would use a (2​n+1)(2n+1)th probe.

Proposition 4.7.

The algorithm just described makes at most 4​n+14n+1 value queries, all on subsets of arrived elements, and accepts at most kk elements. For μ\mu-monotone ff and T>0T>0, it satisfies

𝔼⁡[f⁡(A)]≥[(1−p)​Λμ​(T)−200(k+1)3−e−(2​ln⁡2−1)​n]​OPT.\mathbb{E}[f(A)]\geq\Bigl[(1-p)\Lambda_{\mu}(T)-\frac{200}{(k+1)^{3}}-e^{-(2\ln 2-1)n}\Bigr]\mathrm{OPT}.
Proof.

Ignore the probe limit at first. By the Poisson void probability, conditional on the state history, the test of ii passes with probability e−τi​(t)e^{-\tau_{i}(t)}, and PiP_{i} is independent of all other randomness. By induction over arrivals, the execution has the same distribution as that with uniforms UiU_{i}, so Theorem 3.1 applies.

The processes together have a Poisson⁡(n)\mathrm{Poisson}(n) number of points, which exceeds 2​n2n with probability at most e−(2​ln⁡2−1)​ne^{-(2\ln 2-1)n} by the Chernoff bound. Only on this event does the limit change the output, and it then loses at most OPT\mathrm{OPT}, because the output without the limit is feasible. The query count is one for f⁡(∅)f(\emptyset); one singleton query and one current marginal query per element; and at most 2​n2n probe queries. ∎

5 Beyond 1/e1/e for general objectives

The guarantee 1/e1/e of Theorem 1.1(a) is not the limit for general objectives. In this section we prove the following.

Theorem 5.1.

There is a randomized algorithm that knows only nn and kk, accepts at most kk elements on every execution, makes polynomially many value queries, each on a subset of the elements that have arrived, and satisfies

𝔼⁡[f⁡(A)]≥(1e+3.5⋅10−6−o⁡(1))​OPT\mathbb{E}[f(A)]\geq\Bigl(\frac{1}{e}+3.5\cdot 10^{-6}-o(1)\Bigr)\mathrm{OPT}

for every nonnegative submodular ff, where o⁡(1)o(1) tends to zero as k→∞k\to\infty, uniformly in n≥kn\geq k and ff.

The gain is tiny, and we make no attempt to optimize it; the point is that 1/e1/e is not the answer. The algorithm flips a biased coin and runs one of two algorithms. Their guarantees depend on one parameter of the instance, which neither algorithm computes. Let W=OPT>0W=\mathrm{OPT}>0, and define the excess

d=1Wmax{f(X)+f(Y):X∩Y=∅,|X|,|Y|≤k}−1.d=\frac{1}{W}\max\bigl\{f(X)+f(Y):X\cap Y=\emptyset,\ |X|,|Y|\leq k\bigr\}-1.

Taking XX optimal and Y=∅Y=\emptyset shows d≥0d\geq 0, and d≤1d\leq 1 since each term is at most WW. If dd is large, there are two disjoint sets of nearly optimal value, and a variant of AttenuatedPricing can compare its progress against both of them at the start, which yields more than 1/e1/e. If dd is small, then every feasible set disjoint from an optimal set is worth little, so elements outside the optimum do little harm, and a rule close to Greedy, restricted to a pool of promising elements, does much better than 1/e1/e. A suitable mixture of the two cancels the dependence on dd.

5.1 Two comparators

Fix a switch time ζ∈[0,1/2)\zeta\in[0,1/2) and let χ(t)=1+𝟏[t<ζ]\chi(t)=1+\mathbf{1}[t<\zeta]. The algorithm AttenuatedPricingζ\textsc{AttenuatedPricing}_{\zeta} is AttenuatedPricing with three changes, which make it pay for two comparators before time ζ\zeta:

  • •

    the horizon is Tζ=T−ζT_{\zeta}=T-\zeta, where TT is as in Section 3;

  • •

    the integrating factor is h(t)=exp(−∫tTζχ(v)dv)h(t)=\exp\bigl(-\int_{t}^{T_{\zeta}}\chi(v)\,dv\bigr);

  • •

    the price within an epoch that started at time ss is θt=h​(t)−1​M​exp⁡(λ⁡(j−b)−κ​∫stχ⁡(v)​𝑑v)\theta_{t}=h(t)^{-1}M\exp\bigl(\lambda(j-b)-\kappa\int_{s}^{t}\chi(v)\,dv\bigr).

For ζ=0\zeta=0 this is AttenuatedPricing. Since h≤1h\leq 1 and hh increases, prices are still nonincreasing between state changes.

Lemma 5.2.

Let ζ∈[0,1/2)\zeta\in[0,1/2), and suppose that Tζ>ζT_{\zeta}>\zeta. For every nonnegative submodular ff with excess dd, AttenuatedPricingζ\textsc{AttenuatedPricing}_{\zeta} accepts at most kk elements and

𝔼⁡[f⁡(A)]≥[(1−p)​e−Tζ​((1+d)​(1−e−ζ)+Tζ−ζ)−200(k+1)3]​W.\mathbb{E}[f(A)]\geq\Bigl[(1-p)\,e^{-T_{\zeta}}\bigl((1+d)(1-e^{-\zeta})+T_{\zeta}-\zeta\bigr)-\frac{200}{(k+1)^{3}}\Bigr]W.

In particular, 𝔼⁡[f⁡(A)]≥(hζ+uζ​d−o⁡(1))​W\mathbb{E}[f(A)]\geq(h_{\zeta}+u_{\zeta}d-o(1))W, where hζ=((2−2​ζ)​eζ−1)/eh_{\zeta}=((2-2\zeta)e^{\zeta}-1)/e and uζ=(eζ−1)/eu_{\zeta}=(e^{\zeta}-1)/e.

We follow Section 4. Lemma 4.1 and Lemma 4.2 hold without change, since they use only the structure of the decisions. Apply Lemma 4.2 with the set X′∪Y′X^{\prime}\cup Y^{\prime} and the weight ψ=h 1[t<ζ]\psi=h\,\mathbf{1}[t<\zeta], and again with the set OO and the weight ψ=h 1[t≥ζ]\psi=h\,\mathbf{1}[t\geq\zeta], and add the two inequalities. Before time ζ\zeta, submodularity gives ∑i∈X′∪Y′zi​(t)≥f⁡(At∪X′)+f⁡(At∪Y′)−2​f​(At)−2​k​θt\sum_{i\in X^{\prime}\cup Y^{\prime}}z_{i}(t)\geq f(A_{t}\cup X^{\prime})+f(A_{t}\cup Y^{\prime})-2f(A_{t})-2k\theta_{t}, and after ζ\zeta the bound is as in Lemma 4.3. 𝔼0​[f⁡(ATζ)]≥∫0ζh⁡(t)​e−t​(f⁡(X′)+f⁡(Y′))​𝑑t+∫ζTζh⁡(t)​e−t​f​(O)​𝑑t+𝔼0​[∫h​θ​𝑑N−k​∫χ​h​θ​𝑑t].\mathbb{E}_{0}[f(A_{T_{\zeta}})]\geq\int_{0}^{\zeta}h(t)e^{-t}\bigl(f(X^{\prime})+f(Y^{\prime})\bigr)\,dt+\int_{\zeta}^{T_{\zeta}}h(t)e^{-t}f(O)\,dt+\mathbb{E}_{0}\Bigl[\int h\theta\,dN-k\int\chi h\theta\,dt\Bigr].

Here h⁡(t)​e−t=et−ζ−Tζh(t)e^{-t}=e^{t-\zeta-T_{\zeta}} for t<ζt<\zeta and h⁡(t)​e−t=e−Tζh(t)e^{-t}=e^{-T_{\zeta}} for t≥ζt\geq\zeta, so the two integrals equal e−Tζ​(1−e−ζ)​(f⁡(X′)+f⁡(Y′))e^{-T_{\zeta}}(1-e^{-\zeta})(f(X^{\prime})+f(Y^{\prime})) and e−Tζ​(Tζ−ζ)​f​(O)e^{-T_{\zeta}}(T_{\zeta}-\zeta)f(O). In Lemma 4.4, the potential Ψ\Psi now decreases at rate κ​χ​Ψ=k​χ​ψ\kappa\chi\Psi=k\chi\psi, so part (a) holds with k​∫χ​h​θ​𝑑tk\int\chi h\theta\,dt in place of k​∫h​θ​𝑑tk\int h\theta\,dt, and in part (b) an epoch [s,s′)[s,s^{\prime}) contains at most ν​k​∫ss′χ+b+1\nu k\int_{s}^{s^{\prime}}\chi+b+1 normal acceptances. As ∫0Tζχ=Tζ+ζ=T\int_{0}^{T_{\zeta}}\chi=T_{\zeta}+\zeta=T, the count bound B≤k+(b+2)​(D−m)B\leq k+(b+2)(D-m) is unchanged, and so are Lemma 4.5 and the error terms of Section 4.5. Finally, Lemma 2.1 applied to S↦f⁡(X∖S)S\mapsto f(X\setminus S), and likewise for YY and O∗O^{*}, gives 𝔼⁡[f⁡(X′)+f⁡(Y′)]≥(1−p)​(1+d)​W\mathbb{E}[f(X^{\prime})+f(Y^{\prime})]\geq(1-p)(1+d)W and 𝔼​f​(O)≥(1−p)​W\mathbb{E}f(O)\geq(1-p)W. For ζ=0\zeta=0 this is 1/e1/e, and for small ζ>0\zeta>0 we have hζ=1e​(1−ζ2+O⁡(ζ3))h_{\zeta}=\frac{1}{e}(1-\zeta^{2}+O(\zeta^{3})) and uζ≥ζ/eu_{\zeta}\geq\zeta/e, so AttenuatedPricingζ\textsc{AttenuatedPricing}_{\zeta} beats 1/e1/e by a first-order amount whenever dd is not tiny.

5.2 Structure when the excess is small

Fix an optimal set OO, so that |O|≤k|O|\leq k and f⁡(O)=Wf(O)=W, and order its elements as o1,o2,…o_{1},o_{2},\dots. Let voi=f⁡(oi∣{o1,…,oi−1})v_{o_{i}}=f(o_{i}\mid\{o_{1},\dots,o_{i-1}\}) and v⁡(J)=∑o∈Jvov(J)=\sum_{o\in J}v_{o} for J⊆OJ\subseteq O.

Lemma 5.3.

The weights vov_{o} are nonnegative, v⁡(O)=W−f⁡(∅)v(O)=W-f(\emptyset), and:

  1. (a)

    f⁡(J)≥f⁡(∅)+v⁡(J)f(J)\geq f(\emptyset)+v(J) for all J⊆OJ\subseteq O, and f⁡(J)≤f⁡(J′)f(J)\leq f(J^{\prime}) whenever J⊆J′⊆OJ\subseteq J^{\prime}\subseteq O;

  2. (b)

    f⁡(X)≤v⁡(X∩O)+d​Wf(X)\leq v(X\cap O)+dW for every XX with |X|≤k|X|\leq k;

  3. (c)

    f⁡(X)≤max⁡{1,|X|/k}​d​Wf(X)\leq\max\{1,|X|/k\}\,dW for every XX disjoint from OO.

Proof.

For J⊆OJ\subseteq O and o∈O∖Jo\in O\setminus J, submodularity and the optimality of OO give f⁡(o∣J)≥f⁡(o∣O∖{o})=W−f⁡(O∖{o})≥0f(o\mid J)\geq f(o\mid O\setminus\{o\})=W-f(O\setminus\{o\})\geq 0. This proves nonnegativity and the monotonicity in (a), and the bound f⁡(J)−f⁡(∅)≥v⁡(J)f(J)-f(\emptyset)\geq v(J) follows by adding the elements of JJ in the order of OO and using submodularity. For (b), the sets XX and O∖XO\setminus X are disjoint and have at most kk elements, so f⁡(X)+f⁡(O∖X)≤(1+d)​Wf(X)+f(O\setminus X)\leq(1+d)W, while by (a) f⁡(O∖X)≥f⁡(∅)+v⁡(O)−v⁡(X∩O)=W−v⁡(X∩O)f(O\setminus X)\geq f(\emptyset)+v(O)-v(X\cap O)=W-v(X\cap O). For (c), if |X|≤k|X|\leq k then (b) gives f⁡(X)≤d​Wf(X)\leq dW. If |X|>k|X|>k, let RR be a uniformly random kk-subset of XX. Lemma 2.1, applied to Z↦f⁡(X∖Z)Z\mapsto f(X\setminus Z) with the random set X∖RX\setminus R, gives 𝔼​f​(R)≥k|X|​f​(X)\mathbb{E}f(R)\geq\frac{k}{|X|}f(X), while f⁡(R)≤d​Wf(R)\leq dW. ∎

5.3 A pruned Greedy

Fix parameters η∈(0,1/2)\eta\in(0,1/2), ρ>1−η\rho>1-\eta, t2∈(0,1)t_{2}\in(0,1), t1∈(0,c)t_{1}\in(0,c) where c=1−1−t22c=1-\sqrt{1-t_{2}^{2}}, and σ>1\sigma>1, such that ρ​t1+σ⁡(t2−t1)<1\rho t_{1}+\sigma(t_{2}-t_{1})<1. Let

g=t2−c,K=max{1,(1−η)2ρ​η},ω=k−1/4,b0=⌈k⌉,λ0=ln⁡(k+1)b0,g=t_{2}-c,\qquad K=\max\Bigl\{1,\frac{(1-\eta)^{2}}{\rho\eta}\Bigr\},\qquad\omega=k^{-1/4},\qquad b_{0}=\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil,\qquad\lambda_{0}=\frac{\ln(k+1)}{b_{0}},

and, for a scale M≥0M\geq 0, let Φ​(z)=Mk​(eλ0​z−1λ0−z)\Phi(z)=\frac{M}{k}\bigl(\frac{e^{\lambda_{0}z}-1}{\lambda_{0}}-z\bigr) for z≥0z\geq 0, so that Φ′​(z)=Mk​(eλ0​z−1)\Phi^{\prime}(z)=\frac{M}{k}(e^{\lambda_{0}z}-1). Fix a total order on EE, used to break ties.

PrunedGreedy. Each element has an independent uniform timestamp.

  1. 1.

    Training. Reject every element with timestamp below η\eta, and let SS be the set of these elements and MM the largest singleton value among them, or 00 if there are none. Starting from B=∅B=\emptyset, repeatedly add to BB the element of S∖BS\setminus B with the largest marginal f⁡(i∣B)f(i\mid B), ties broken by the fixed order, as long as this marginal is positive and |B|<k|B|<k. The set BB is not accepted.

  2. 2.

    Validation. The score of an element i∉Si\notin S is f⁡(i∣B)f(i\mid B), and its key is the pair formed by its score and its position in the fixed order, compared lexicographically. Reject every element with timestamp in [η,η′)[\eta,\eta^{\prime}), where η′=η+ω⁡(1−η)\eta^{\prime}=\eta+\omega(1-\eta), and let VV be the set of these elements. Let mV=⌊ω​ρ​k⌋m_{V}=\lfloor\omega\rho k\rfloor. If VV contains at least mVm_{V} elements of positive score, let κ^\hat{\kappa} be the mVm_{V}th largest key among them; otherwise let κ^\hat{\kappa} be smaller than every key. An element with timestamp after η′\eta^{\prime} is in the pool PP if its score is positive and its key exceeds κ^\hat{\kappa}.

  3. 3.

    Live phase. Rescale the time after η′\eta^{\prime} to x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1]. Reject every arrival outside the pool. A pool element arriving at time xx, with w=f⁡(i∣A)w=f(i\mid A) against the current accepted set AA, is accepted as follows. If x≤t1x\leq t_{1}, accept it if and only if w>0w>0. If t1<x≤t2t_{1}<x\leq t_{2} and f⁡({i})>Mf(\{i\})>M, accept it if and only if w>0w>0. If t1<x≤t2t_{1}<x\leq t_{2} and f⁡({i})≤Mf(\{i\})\leq M, accept it if and only if w>Φ′​(Qx−)w>\Phi^{\prime}(Q_{x^{-}}), and then increase QQ by one. Here the queue QQ starts at 00 at time t1t_{1} and decreases at rate σ​k\sigma k while it is positive. Reject all arrivals after time t2t_{2}, and all arrivals once kk elements have been accepted.

The training step uses O⁡(n​k)O(nk) queries on subsets of SS, and every later query is on B∪{i}B\cup\{i\} or A∪{i}A\cup\{i\} for an arrived element ii. Elements with f⁡({i})>Mf(\{i\})>M are exceptional, and the others are normal. The algorithm never needs OO, WW, or dd.

Lemma 5.4.

Let D=O∩PD=O\cap P. Then 𝔼​f​(D)≥(1−2​η−(1+K)​d−o⁡(1))​W\mathbb{E}f(D)\geq(1-2\eta-(1+K)d-o(1))W. Moreover, with probability 1−o⁡(1)1-o(1), |P|≤(ρ+o⁡(1))​k|P|\leq(\rho+o(1))k and fewer than k\sqrt{k} elements outside SS are exceptional. Here, and in the rest of this section, o⁡(1)o(1) tends to zero as k→∞k\to\infty uniformly in nn and ff.

Proof.

The pool. List the elements outside SS with positive score in decreasing order of key, and let JRJ_{R} consist of the first RR of them, or all of them if there are fewer. Let R±=⌊(ρ±k−1/8)k⌋R_{\pm}=\lfloor(\rho\pm k^{-1/8})k\rfloor. Given SS, which determines all scores, each element outside SS lies in VV independently with probability ω\omega. The number of elements of JR−J_{R_{-}} in VV is binomial with mean at most ω​R−≤mV−k5/8+1\omega R_{-}\leq m_{V}-k^{5/8}+1 and variance at most ω​ρ​k=O⁡(k3/4)\omega\rho k=O(k^{3/4}), so by Chernoff’s bound it is below mVm_{V} with probability 1−o⁡(1)1-o(1); in that case every element of JR−J_{R_{-}} has key above κ^\hat{\kappa}, and so JR−∖V⊆PJ_{R_{-}}\setminus V\subseteq P. In the same way, if there are at least R+R_{+} positive scores then JR+J_{R_{+}} contains at least mVm_{V} elements of VV with probability 1−o⁡(1)1-o(1), so that P⊆JR+P\subseteq J_{R_{+}}; and if there are fewer, then P⊆JR+P\subseteq J_{R_{+}} trivially. So with probability 1−o⁡(1)1-o(1) we have JR−∖V⊆P⊆JR+J_{R_{-}}\setminus V\subseteq P\subseteq J_{R_{+}}, and in particular |P|≤(ρ+o⁡(1))​k|P|\leq(\rho+o(1))k. For the exceptional elements, rank all elements by singleton value, with ties broken by the fixed order; the exceptional elements outside SS are those ranked above every element of SS, and there are at least ll of them with probability at most (1−η)l(1-\eta)^{l}.

We generate SS by independent coins: i∈Si\in S if and only if the coin of ii shows heads, which has probability η\eta. Consider the following scan. It maintains a set HH of heads, initially empty. At each step, among the elements whose coin has not been revealed, it takes the one with the largest key with respect to HH, that is, the largest pair of marginal f⁡(i∣H)f(i\mid H) and position in the fixed order; if this marginal is not positive it stops, and otherwise it reveals the coin, adding the element to HH on heads. Remark 5.7.

The o⁡(1)o(1) terms decay slowly; for example, the validation step costs a term of order k−1/8k^{-1/8}, and so the guarantee exceeds 1/e1/e only for astronomically large kk. The proof is designed to show that 1/e1/e is not the limit, and we have not tried to obtain a useful explicit threshold. The mechanism is that dd measures how much two disjoint feasible sets can be worth together: AttenuatedPricingζ\textsc{AttenuatedPricing}_{\zeta} profits from a large dd, and PrunedGreedy from a small one.

6 Hardness for monotone coverage functions

We now prove Theorem 1.2. The construction adapts the probability-coverage idea from Section 3 of Udwani and Wajc [UW26], who study submodular welfare, to a single cardinality constraint with random arrivals.

Theorem 6.1.

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a randomized online algorithm with unlimited computation and queries on arrived elements. Write gr​(x)=1−(1−1/r)xg_{r}(x)=1-(1-1/r)^{x}.

Moreover, for every ε>0\varepsilon>0 there is an instance on which the ratio is at most gk​(k)+εg_{k}(k)+\varepsilon.

  2. (b)

    For every k≥64k\geq 64, let r≥2r\geq 2 be the largest integer with r3​r≤kr^{3r}\leq k. Since r=Θ⁡(log⁡k/log⁡log⁡k)r=\Theta(\log k/\log\log k) and gr​(r)≤1−1/e+1/(2​e​(r−1))g_{r}(r)\leq 1-1/e+1/(2e(r-1)), this is at most 1−1/e+O⁡(log⁡log⁡k/log⁡k)1-1/e+O(\log\log k/\log k).

Fix integers r,R≥2r,R\geq 2 and ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1, and let

7 Hardness for general objectives

The instances of Section 6 are monotone, and AttenuatedPricing achieves 1−1/e−o⁡(1)1-1/e-o(1) on them. We now show that nonmonotonicity by itself creates a stronger barrier: we prove the barrier 12\frac{1}{2} of Theorem 1.5(a), and then a bound strictly below 12\frac{1}{2}. The constant 0.4970530.497053 of part (b) is proved in Appendix C. The building block is a pair of elements that are valuable separately and worthless together, where the ratio between the two values is hidden on a long geometric scale.

7.1 The basic barrier

Theorem 7.1.

Let n≥2n\geq 2, 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n, μ∈[0,1]\mu\in[0,1], and ε>0\varepsilon>0. There is a finite family of normalized, nonnegative, μ\mu-monotone submodular functions on nn elements such that, for every algorithm with unlimited computation, unlimited queries on arrived elements, and full knowledge of the family, some member ff satisfies 𝔼⁡[f⁡(A)]≤(1+μ2+ε)​OPT\mathbb{E}[f(A)]\leq\bigl(\frac{1+\mu}{2}+\varepsilon\bigr)\mathrm{OPT}.

f⁡(∅)=0,f⁡({a})=KJ,f⁡({b})=KJ+1,f⁡({a,b})=μ​KJ+1.f(\emptyset)=0,\qquad f(\{a\})=K^{J},\qquad f(\{b\})=K^{J+1},\qquad f(\{a,b\})=\mu K^{J+1}.

Since k≥1k\geq 1, its optimum is OPT=KJ+1\mathrm{OPT}=K^{J+1}, attained by {b}\{b\}.

Draw (a,b)(a,b) and JJ uniformly, independently of the arrival order. It suffices to bound the average of 𝔼⁡[f⁡(A)]/OPT\mathbb{E}[f(A)]/\mathrm{OPT} over this prior by 1+μ2+ε\frac{1+\mu}{2}+\varepsilon, and by linearity we may assume that the algorithm is deterministic. Condition on the arrival order and on the unordered pair {a,b}\{a,b\}. Let e1e_{1} be the member of the pair arriving first and e2e_{2} the other. Until e2e_{2} arrives, every allowed query on a set SS returns v 1[e1∈S]v\,\mathbf{1}[e_{1}\in S], where v=f⁡({e1})v=f(\{e_{1}\}). (N−1)​(1+μ+1/K)+22​N≤1+μ2+12​K+12​N≤1+μ2+ε.∎\frac{(N-1)(1+\mu+1/K)+2}{2N}\leq\frac{1+\mu}{2}+\frac{1}{2K}+\frac{1}{2N}\leq\frac{1+\mu}{2}+\varepsilon.\qed

7.2 Below one half

We now show that the limiting ratio for general objectives is strictly below 1/21/2. The pairs are kept, but a small fraction of the value is moved into a matroid gadget in which a second, “bad” basis interferes with a “good” one.

Let 𝖬\mathsf{M} be a matroid of rank r≥1r\geq 1 with rank function r𝖬r_{\mathsf{M}}, whose ground set is the disjoint union of two bases GG and BB; parallel elements are allowed and are distinct. Let

φ𝖬​(S)=r𝖬​(S)−|S∩B|.\varphi_{\mathsf{M}}(S)=r_{\mathsf{M}}(S)-|S\cap B|.

Its maximum is φ𝖬​(G)=r\varphi_{\mathsf{M}}(G)=r. Then 𝒯\mathcal{T} is a basis, and we define the greedy retention

β⁡(𝖬,G,B)=1r​𝔼​|𝒯∩G|=1−1r​𝔼​|𝒯∩B|.\beta(\mathsf{M};G,B)=\frac{1}{r}\mathbb{E}|\mathcal{T}\cap G|=1-\frac{1}{r}\mathbb{E}|\mathcal{T}\cap B|.

If β<1/2\beta<1/2, then C⁡(β)=2−2​β+β−1<1/2C(\beta)=\sqrt{2-2\beta}+\beta-1<1/2, since C⁡(1/2)=1/2C(1/2)=1/2 and C′(β)=1−(2−2β)−1/2>0C^{\prime}(\beta)=1-(2-2\beta)^{-1/2}>0 for β<1/2\beta<1/2.

Theorem 7.2.

Let (𝖬,G,B)(\mathsf{M};G,B) be as above, with β=β⁡(𝖬,G,B)<1/2\beta=\beta(\mathsf{M};G,B)<1/2, and let ε>0\varepsilon>0. There is a finite family ℱ\mathcal{F} of normalized, nonnegative, submodular functions on a common ground set of size n0n_{0}, such that the following holds for every algorithm with unlimited computation, unlimited queries on arrived elements, and full knowledge of ℱ\mathcal{F}, even if it observes the arrival times. Corollary 7.3.

For every sufficiently large kk, no online algorithm, even with unlimited computation and queries, has ratio more than 0.499990.49999 with budget kk. More precisely, the best ratio ρk\rho_{k} satisfies lim supk→∞ρk≤91/90−91/180<0.4999847\limsup_{k\to\infty}\rho_{k}\leq\sqrt{91/90}-91/180<0.4999847.

Proof.

Let 𝖬\mathsf{M} be the graphic matroid on the vertices {0,1,2,3}\{0,1,2,3\}, with G={01,02,03}G=\{01,02,03\} and B={01′,12,23}B=\{01^{\prime},12,23\}, where 0101 and 01′01^{\prime} are parallel edges. Both are spanning trees, hence bases of rank 33. Fix g∈Gg\in G. With one large fan per level instead of many small gadgets, a finer analysis of the same construction gives a better constant (Appendix C).

Theorem 1.5 now follows: part (a) is Theorem 7.1; part (b) follows from Theorem C.10 in Appendix C with ε=10−7\varepsilon=10^{-7}, since Cblk+10−7<0.497053C_{\mathrm{blk}}+10^{-7}<0.497053.

The model in the proof.

We strengthen the algorithm: after each arrival it is told the entire table of values f⁡(S)f(S) for all sets SS of arrived elements, and it observes independent uniform arrival times. Since a randomized algorithm is a mixture of deterministic ones, it suffices to bound, for every deterministic algorithm, the expected instancewise ratio 𝔼⁡[f⁡(A)/OPT⁡(f)]\mathbb{E}[f(A)/\mathrm{OPT}(f)] when ff is drawn from a distribution on ℱ\mathcal{F}; some member of ℱ\mathcal{F} then has expected ratio at most the same bound. In the construction, OPT⁡(f)\mathrm{OPT}(f) is attained by a set of at most n0n_{0} elements, so the budget never binds when k≥n0k\geq n_{0}. Adding k−n0k-n_{0} elements of value zero, whose arrivals the algorithm could simulate itself, gives instances of size exactly kk.

The construction.

Fix a rational δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2), integers N≥1N\geq 1 and m>2​Nm>2N, and an integer YY that is a multiple of rr; at the end Y→∞Y\to\infty. Let ℋN=∑d=1N1/d\mathcal{H}_{N}=\sum_{d=1}^{N}1/d and πd=1/(d​ℋN)\pi_{d}=1/(d\mathcal{H}_{N}), so that ∑d≤Nπd=1\sum_{d\leq N}\pi_{d}=1. Let QQ be the least multiple of Q0=den⁡(δ)​num​(ℋN)​N!Q_{0}=\mathrm{den}(\delta)\,\mathrm{num}(\mathcal{H}_{N})\,N! with Q≥(log⁡Y)2Q\geq(\log Y)^{2}, so that Q<(log⁡Y)2+Q0Q<(\log Y)^{2}+Q_{0}; this makes (1−δ)​Q​πd(1-\delta)Q\pi_{d}, δ​Q\delta Q, and δ​Q​πd\delta Q\pi_{d} integers.

The elements, which we call items, are partitioned into levels 1,…,m1,\dots,m, where level jj has njn_{j} items and njn_{j} is a multiple of rr. The objective is defined on finer objects called atoms, each of which is carried by exactly one item; the value of a set of items is the value of the set of atoms they carry. Each item of level jj carries QQ good atoms of weight uj=1/(nj​Q)u_{j}=1/(n_{j}Q). Atoms are grouped into components, and ff is the sum of the component values.

  • •

    For j≤Nj\leq N, the good atoms of level jj form a single modular component with value uj​|S|u_{j}|S|.

  • •

    For j>Nj>N, each item owns (1−δ)​Q(1-\delta)Q pair components. Each consists of one of its good atoms gg and a bad atom bb, with value uj​𝟏​[g∈S,b∉S]u_{j}\mathbf{1}[g\in S,\,b\notin S]; this is uj​φu_{j}\varphi for the rank-one matroid in which gg and bb are parallel.

  • •

    For j>Nj>N, the items of level jj are partitioned into groups of rr, and each group has δ​Q\delta Q copies of 𝖬\mathsf{M}, with value uj​φ𝖬u_{j}\varphi_{\mathsf{M}} each. The good elements of each copy are good atoms of the rr items of the group, one for each item, and its bad elements are bad atoms. Let 𝖬j\mathsf{M}_{j} be the direct sum of all copies at level jj; it has rank Rj=δ​nj​QR_{j}=\delta n_{j}Q.

Bad atoms of level j>Nj>N are carried by items of the lower levels j−dj-d, 1≤d≤N1\leq d\leq N. For each item of level jj and each dd, exactly (1−δ)​Q​πd(1-\delta)Q\pi_{d} of its pair components have their bad atom sent to level j−dj-d; and exactly δ​nj​Q​πd\delta n_{j}Q\pi_{d} of the bad atoms of 𝖬j\mathsf{M}_{j} are sent to level j−dj-d, by a fixed rule. Level ℓ\ell then receives

sℓ=∑j>N, 1≤j−ℓ≤Nnj​Q​πj−ℓs_{\ell}=\sum_{j>N,\ 1\leq j-\ell\leq N}n_{j}Q\pi_{j-\ell}

bad atoms, and they are assigned to its items by a uniformly random injection, independently over ℓ\ell. So each item carries its own good atoms and at most one bad atom. The family ℱ\mathcal{F} consists of the objectives obtained from all choices of the injections. Finally, choose the sizes downward: nm=Yn_{m}=Y and nℓ=r⁡⌈Y2​(1+sℓ)2/r⌉n_{\ell}=r\lceil Y^{2}(1+s_{\ell})^{2}/r\rceil for ℓ=m−1,…,1\ell=m-1,\dots,1, which is possible because sℓs_{\ell} depends only on njn_{j} for j>ℓj>\ell. Then

sℓnℓ≤14​Y2,minjnj≥Y,log∑jnj=O(logY),\frac{s_{\ell}}{n_{\ell}}\leq\frac{1}{4Y^{2}},\qquad\min_{j}n_{j}\geq Y,\qquad\log\sum_{j}n_{j}=O(\log Y), (6)

where the last bound follows by induction, as each nℓn_{\ell} is polynomial in Y​Q​∑j>ℓnjYQ\sum_{j>\ell}n_{j}. Here and below, O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot) and o⁡(1)o(1) refer to Y→∞Y\to\infty with δ\delta, NN, mm, and 𝖬\mathsf{M} fixed, and they are uniform over algorithms.

Lemma 7.4.

Every f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} is normalized, nonnegative, and submodular, every item of level jj has singleton value 1/nj≤1/Y1/n_{j}\leq 1/Y, and m⁡(1−1/(4​Y2))≤OPT⁡(f)≤mm(1-1/(4Y^{2}))\leq\mathrm{OPT}(f)\leq m.

Proof.

Each component is uj​φu_{j}\varphi for a matroid with an independent set of bad elements, or modular, and so it is normalized, nonnegative, and submodular. The map from sets of items to sets of atoms preserves unions and intersections, so composing with it preserves submodularity. An item’s good atoms lie in distinct components or are independent in their copy of 𝖬\mathsf{M}, so they contribute uj​Q=1/nju_{j}Q=1/n_{j}; a bad atom alone contributes zero. The total weighted rank of the components of level jj is uj​nj​Q=1u_{j}n_{j}Q=1, so f≤mf\leq m. The items that carry no bad atom have value ∑j(nj−sj)/nj≥m⁡(1−1/(4​Y2))\sum_{j}(n_{j}-s_{j})/n_{j}\geq m(1-1/(4Y^{2})) by (6). ∎

The singleton bound in Theorem 7.2 follows. Arrival times are attached to items, and an atom arrives with its carrier. Let Aj​(t)A_{j}(t) be the number of accepted items of level jj with arrival time at most tt, divided by njn_{j}, and let Pj=Aj​(1)P_{j}=A_{j}(1) and P¯=1m​∑jPj\bar{P}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j}P_{j}.

A relaxation.

For j>Nj>N, let 𝒯j\mathcal{T}_{j} be the set of bad atoms of 𝖬j\mathsf{M}_{j} that increase the rank of the set of all atoms of 𝖬j\mathsf{M}_{j} that arrived before them. Since 𝖬j\mathsf{M}_{j} is a direct sum, this can be decided in each copy of 𝖬\mathsf{M} separately, and within a copy no two atoms arrive together, as shown below. So 𝒯j\mathcal{T}_{j} is well defined, and it depends only on the instance and the arrival times, not on the algorithm. Let f¯\bar{f} be obtained from ff by deleting from their components all bad atoms of 𝖬j\mathsf{M}_{j} outside 𝒯j\mathcal{T}_{j}, for every jj, and every bad atom of a pair component whose carrier arrives after the item owning the good atom. Since r𝖬​(S)≤r𝖬​(S∖{b})+1r_{\mathsf{M}}(S)\leq r_{\mathsf{M}}(S\setminus\{b\})+1, deleting a bad element never decreases φ𝖬\varphi_{\mathsf{M}}, and so f≤f¯f\leq\bar{f} pointwise. We bound 𝔼​[f¯​(A)]\mathbb{E}[\bar{f}(A)].

In each copy of 𝖬\mathsf{M}, the 2​r2r atoms have distinct carriers: the good ones by construction, the bad ones because the injections are injective, and good and bad carriers lie in different levels. So their relative order is uniformly random, and 𝔼​|𝒯j|=(nj/r)​δ​Q⋅r⁡(1−β)\mathbb{E}|\mathcal{T}_{j}|=(n_{j}/r)\,\delta Q\cdot r(1-\beta). If BA⊆𝒯jB_{A}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{j} is the set of atoms of 𝒯j\mathcal{T}_{j} carried by accepted items, then the matroid part of level jj contributes at most uj​(Rj−|BA|)=uj​(Rj−|𝒯j|)+uj​|𝒯j∖BA|u_{j}(R_{j}-|B_{A}|)=u_{j}(R_{j}-|\mathcal{T}_{j}|)+u_{j}|\mathcal{T}_{j}\setminus B_{A}| to f¯​(A)\bar{f}(A), and

𝔼⁡[uj​(Rj−|𝒯j|)]=δ​β.\mathbb{E}\bigl[u_{j}(R_{j}-|\mathcal{T}_{j}|)\bigr]=\delta\beta. (7)

Invisible roles.

An atom b∈𝒯jb\in\mathcal{T}_{j} increases the rank of every subset of the atoms of 𝖬j\mathsf{M}_{j} that arrived before it, by submodularity of rank, and so it has zero marginal value in its component on every set of atoms that have arrived when it arrives. Thus deleting bb does not change any value that the algorithm has observed up to and including the arrival of its carrier; we say that bb is invisible at arrival. Similarly, the bad atom of a pair component is invisible until the good atom arrives, since a pair containing only its bad atom has value zero.

Lemma 7.5.

Fix a level ℓ\ell, and a fixed set of ww among the sℓs_{\ell} bad atoms sent to level ℓ\ell. Let XX be the number of these atoms that are invisible at arrival and whose carrier is rejected. Then, for every algorithm, 𝔼​X≤w​𝔼​[1−Pℓ]+w​sℓ/nℓ+2​w\mathbb{E}X\leq w\,\mathbb{E}[1-P_{\ell}]+ws_{\ell}/n_{\ell}+2\sqrt{w}.

Proof.

Condition on all randomness other than the injection σ\sigma into level ℓ\ell, including all arrival times and the injections into other levels; σ\sigma remains uniform. Let ν=nℓ\nu=n_{\ell}, and let the items of level ℓ\ell arrive in the order 1,…,ν1,\dots,\nu. Reveal which atom item ii carries only after the decision on item ii. Every value observed up to then involves only arrived items, and so is determined by what has been revealed. Given the revealed information, the unrevealed atoms are injected uniformly into the s=ν−i+1s=\nu-i+1 items that have not yet been decided, which include item ii.

Let Zi∈{0,1}Z_{i}\in\{0,1\} indicate that item ii is rejected, and let Zi0Z_{i}^{0} indicate whether the algorithm would reject item ii if the bad atom carried by item ii were deleted from the values observed at its arrival. Then Zi0Z^{0}_{i} is determined before the atom carried by item ii is revealed, and Zi=Zi0Z_{i}=Z_{i}^{0} whenever item ii carries an invisible atom. Let YsY_{s} be the number of the ww fixed atoms not yet revealed. Each lands on item ii with conditional probability 1/s1/s, and so

Since the arrival times are fixed by the conditioning, YsY_{s} counts the fixed atoms that land in a fixed set of ss items, so it has mean w​s/νws/\nu and, by negative correlation, variance at most w​s/νws/\nu. Hence 𝔼​|Ys/s−w/ν|≤w/(ν​s)\mathbb{E}|Y_{s}/s-w/\nu|\leq\sqrt{w/(\nu s)}, which sums to at most 2​w2\sqrt{w}. Finally, Zi0Z_{i}^{0} and ZiZ_{i} differ only at items that carry a bad atom, of which there are at most sℓs_{\ell}, so ∑iZi0≤ν⁡(1−Pℓ)+sℓ\sum_{i}Z^{0}_{i}\leq\nu(1-P_{\ell})+s_{\ell}. ∎

Every atom of 𝒯j∖BA\mathcal{T}_{j}\setminus B_{A} is invisible at arrival and has a rejected carrier. Apply Lemma 7.5 to the δ​nj​Q​πd\delta n_{j}Q\pi_{d} bad atoms of 𝖬j\mathsf{M}_{j} sent to level j−dj-d, multiply by uju_{j}, and sum over dd. Together with (7) and (6), and using that each level ℓ\ell receives weight πd\pi_{d} from at most one level j=ℓ+dj=\ell+d for each dd, the expected matroid part of f¯​(A)\bar{f}(A) is at most

δ​m​β+δ​∑ℓ=1m𝔼⁡[1−Pℓ]+o⁡(1).\delta m\beta+\delta\sum_{\ell=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}[1-P_{\ell}]+o(1). (8)

Pairs.

Fix an item xx of level j>Nj>N and a distance dd, let ℓ=j−d\ell=j-d, and let q=(1−δ)​Q​πdq=(1-\delta)Q\pi_{d} be the number of pair components of xx whose bad atoms go to level ℓ\ell. Condition on everything except where these qq bad atoms are placed. Before xx arrives, these components are invisible, so the set SℓS_{\ell} of items of level ℓ\ell accepted before xx arrives does not depend on their placement. Given the conditioning, the qq carriers are a uniformly random qq-subset, drawn without replacement, of a set of at least nℓ−sℓn_{\ell}-s_{\ell} items of level ℓ\ell, and so the expected fraction of them in SℓS_{\ell} is at least (|Sℓ|−sℓ)/nℓ(|S_{\ell}|-s_{\ell})/n_{\ell}. On this event, consider an accepted item xx of level jj, arriving at time tt. Thus the expected pair part of f¯​(A)\bar{f}(A) is at most

(1−δ)​𝔼​∑j>N∫(0,1][1−∑d=1Nπd​Aj−d​(t−)]​d​Aj​(t)+o⁡(m).(1-\delta)\,\mathbb{E}\sum_{j>N}\int_{(0,1]}\Bigl[1-\sum_{d=1}^{N}\pi_{d}A_{j-d}(t^{-})\Bigr]dA_{j}(t)+o(m). (9)

Smoothing.

Index the levels cyclically by ℤm\mathbb{Z}_{m}, let (𝖲​x)j=xj−1(\mathsf{S}x)_{j}=x_{j-1}, and let Π=∑d=1Nπd​𝖲d\Pi=\sum_{d=1}^{N}\pi_{d}\mathsf{S}^{d}. As N<m/2N<m/2, the circulant matrix Π\Pi has zero diagonal and row sums one, and for j>Nj>N its row jj is the kernel (πd)(\pi_{d}) used in (9). since the first and last terms lie in [0,2​η′][0,2\eta^{\prime}] and the middle term is subtracted and nonnegative.

We thank Zhiyi Huang and Sahil Singla for helpful discussions, and for joint work on the matroid secretary problem, which led to [ABH+26].

The results in this paper were developed with substantial assistance from AI models, primarily GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.2, working under the direction of the authors, and the manuscript was drafted with the assistance of Claude. The numerical constants in this paper were verified by computer in exact rational or directed-rounding arithmetic.

A Lean 4 formalization, written by GPT-6 Astra, proves every result of this paper. It uses no axioms beyond Lean’s standard ones, except that some of the finite numerical certificates in the appendices are checked with native_decide, which also trusts Lean’s compiler.
