Appendix A Explicit guarantees at every budget

Theorem 3.1 has content only once T>0T>0, which requires kk of order 10710^{7}. This section gives explicit guarantees for general objectives at every budget. Throughout, ff is nonnegative and submodular, but neither monotone nor normalized, and we write W=OPT=max|S|≤k⁡f⁡(S)W=\mathrm{OPT}=\max_{|S|\leq k}f(S) and U=maxi∈E⁡f⁡({i})U=\max_{i\in E}f(\{i\}).

Theorem A.1 (Every budget).

For every k≥1k\geq 1 there is a randomized algorithm that knows only nn and kk, accepts at most kk elements on every execution, makes at most 6​n+16n+1 value queries, each on a subset of the arrived elements, and satisfies 𝔼⁡[f⁡(A)]≥gk​OPT\mathbb{E}[f(A)]\geq g_{k}\mathrm{OPT} for every n≥kn\geq k and every nonnegative submodular ff, where gkg_{k} is given in Table 2. In particular, gk≥0.2677g_{k}\geq 0.2677 for every k≥1k\geq 1, gk≥0.3g_{k}\geq 0.3 for every k≥52k\geq 52, and gk≥0.3678g_{k}\geq 0.3678 for every k≥1012k\geq 10^{12}.

The smallest entry is gk=0.2677g_{k}=0.2677, for 30≤k≤3930\leq k\leq 39; the smallest entries with k≤29k\leq 29 are g28=g29=0.2678g_{28}=g_{29}=0.2678. The policies are of four kinds, which we treat in turn: a two-pick rule for k∈{2,3}k\in\{2,3\} (Section A.1), a multi-rank rule that is restarted after every stop for 4≤k≤294\leq k\leq 29 (Section A.2), and two variants of a Poisson-price policy with eligibility attenuation for k≥30k\geq 30 (Section A.3). For k=1k=1 and as insurance against single large elements we use a classical singleton rule. Each guarantee reduces to a finite computation, which is carried out by computer in exact rational or directed integer arithmetic; no step uses floating point. We assume W>0W>0, since otherwise there is nothing to prove.

Lemma A.2 (Singleton rule).

Fix a total order on EE that refines decreasing singleton values. Reject all arrivals before time 1/e1/e. Afterwards, consider the first arrival that is larger in this order than every earlier arrival (if no element arrived earlier, this is the first arrival); accept it if its singleton value exceeds f⁡(∅)f(\emptyset), and stop in either case. This rule makes n+1n+1 queries, accepts at most one element, and satisfies 𝔼⁡[f⁡(A)]≥U/e\mathbb{E}[f(A)]\geq U/e. If k=1k=1, then 𝔼⁡[f⁡(A)]≥OPT/e\mathbb{E}[f(A)]\geq\mathrm{OPT}/e.

Proof.

Let e∗e^{*} be the largest element, and condition on its timestamp t≥1/et\geq 1/e and on the set of elements that precede it. If this set is empty, e∗e^{*} is the first arrival after 1/e1/e and is considered. Otherwise the largest of its members has a uniform timestamp on [0,t][0,t], and if this timestamp is below 1/e1/e, then no arrival in [1/e,t)[1/e,t) is larger than all earlier arrivals and again e∗e^{*} is considered. So e∗e^{*} is considered with probability at least ∫1/e11e​t​𝑑t=1e\int_{1/e}^{1}\frac{1}{et}\,dt=\frac{1}{e}. If f⁡({e∗})>f⁡(∅)f(\{e^{*}\})>f(\emptyset), it is then accepted, which gives 𝔼​f​(A)≥U/e\mathbb{E}f(A)\geq U/e since all outcomes are nonnegative; if f⁡({e∗})≤f⁡(∅)f(\{e^{*}\})\leq f(\emptyset), then U≤f⁡(∅)≤f⁡(A)U\leq f(\emptyset)\leq f(A) on every execution. For k=1k=1 we have OPT=max⁡{U,f⁡(∅)}\mathrm{OPT}=\max\{U,f(\emptyset)\}, and the same two cases give 𝔼​f​(A)≥OPT/e\mathbb{E}f(A)\geq\mathrm{OPT}/e. ∎

A.2 Restart windows: budgets four to twenty-nine

Add kk virtual elements as in Section A.1; they have independent uniform timestamps, ff ignores them, and they cost no queries. Real and virtual elements are called labels. Fix a grid 0=t0<t1<⋯<tN=10=t_{0}<t_{1}<\dots<t_{N}=1, and call (ti−1,ti](t_{i-1},t_{i}] cell ii. Restart. The algorithm keeps the accepted set SS and the number JJ of stops, and proceeds in rounds; the first round starts at t0=0t_{0}=0 with J=0J=0. A round that starts at a grid point tgt_{g} with J=jJ=j visits the state (g,j)(g,j). If j=kj=k or g=Ng=N, the algorithm ends. Otherwise the round uses the list of (g,j)(g,j), the relative time u=(t−tg)/(1−tg)∈(0,1]u=(t-t_{g})/(1-t_{g})\in(0,1], and b⁡(u)=|{s:xs<u}|b(u)=|\{s:x_{s}<u\}|. It freezes the weights ve=[f⁡(e∣S)]+v_{e}=\left[f(e\mid S)\right]_{+} of all labels not yet arrived (ve=0v_{e}=0 for virtual labels), ordered by decreasing weight with ties broken by a fixed label order. Until a stop occurs in this round:

  • •

    the first arrival whose rank by weight among the round’s arrivals so far, itself included, is at most b⁡(u)b(u) is proposed; it is accepted if its weight is positive, and the proposal is a stop;

  • •

    independently, a stop occurs at rate [b⁡(u)−h⁡(u)]+/u\left[b(u)-h(u)\right]_{+}/u, where h⁡(u)h(u) is the number of arrivals in the round so far, virtual ones included.

If a stop occurs at a time in cell ii, all arrivals up to time tit_{i} are rejected, JJ increases by one, and the next round starts at tit_{i}. If a round has no stop, the algorithm ends.

So each round is a multi-rank secretary rule on the whole remaining horizon, and after a stop it is restarted, at the next grid point, with fresh weights and the list of the new state. The artificial stops are implemented with a private exponential variable compared with the integrated rate, which vanishes before x1x_{1}. At most one element is accepted per stop and there are at most kk stops, so at most kk elements are accepted. The weight of a label is needed only when it arrives during a round, and SS changes only at stops; caching f⁡(S)f(S), which was queried when the last element was accepted, the rule makes at most n+1n+1 queries: f⁡(∅)f(\emptyset) and at most one query f⁡(S∪{e})f(S\cup\{e\}) per real arrival.

The function σ\sigma is continuous and nonincreasing with σ=1\sigma=1 on [0,x1][0,x_{1}], so βi≥0\beta_{i}\geq 0 and ∑iβi=1−σ⁡(1)\sum_{i}\beta_{i}=1-\sigma(1). When the state matters we write ug,iu_{g,i}, βg,j,i\beta_{g,j,i}, ag,j,ia_{g,j,i}, and so on.

Lemma A.7 (Round law).

Consider one round with a fixed list, a fixed finite set of members in a fixed strict order, independent uniform relative times on (0,1](0,1], and independent private randomness.

  1. (i)

    Fix u∈(0,1]u\in(0,1] and a set 𝒬\mathcal{Q} of members. Conditional on 𝒬\mathcal{Q} being the set of members with relative time below uu, and on the relative times of all other members, there is no stop before uu with probability σ⁡(u)\sigma(u).

  2. (ii)

    For every cell ii, conditional on the set of members with relative time above uiu_{i} and on their relative times, a stop occurs in cell ii with probability βi\beta_{i}.

  3. (iii)

    For every member ee and cell ii, conditional on the set of other members with relative time above uiu_{i} and on their relative times, ee is proposed at a relative time in (ui−1,ui](u_{i-1},u_{i}] with probability at most aia_{i}.

  4. (iv)

    The member of rank rr is proposed at a relative time in (ui−1,ui](u_{i-1},u_{i}] with probability τr,i\tau_{r,i}. Moreover, τr,i\tau_{r,i} is nonincreasing in rr, and Ti​(s)≤βiT_{i}(s)\leq\beta_{i} for every s≥0s\geq 0.

Proof.

(i) Let h=|𝒬|h=|\mathcal{Q}|. Given the conditioning, the members of 𝒬\mathcal{Q} have independent uniform relative times on (0,u)(0,u), and they are the only arrivals before uu. Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be the event that for every s≤min⁡(h,b⁡(u))s\leq\min(h,b(u)) the ssth best member of 𝒬\mathcal{Q} arrives no later than xsx_{s}. We claim that there is no eligible arrival (one of rank at most b⁡(⋅)b(\cdot) at its arrival) before uu if and only if 𝒟\mathcal{D} holds. If 𝒟\mathcal{D} fails for ss, the ssth best member of 𝒬\mathcal{Q} arrives at some v∈(xs,u)v\in(x_{s},u), where its rank is at most s≤b⁡(v)s\leq b(v). Conversely, assume 𝒟\mathcal{D} and let y∈𝒬y\in\mathcal{Q} arrive at v<uv<u, with ℓ′=b⁡(v)≤b⁡(u)\ell^{\prime}=b(v)\leq b(u). If ℓ′≤h\ell^{\prime}\leq h, the ℓ′\ell^{\prime} best members of 𝒬\mathcal{Q} arrived no later than x1,…,xℓ′x_{1},\dots,x_{\ell^{\prime}}, all of which are below vv, so yy is not one of them and has rank larger than ℓ′\ell^{\prime}. If ℓ′>h\ell^{\prime}>h, every member of 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, of rank s≤h<ℓ′s\leq h<\ell^{\prime}, arrived no later than xs<vx_{s}<v, which is impossible for yy. This proves the claim, and ℙ⁡[𝒟]=∏s≤min⁡(h,b⁡(u))xs/u\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{D}]=\prod_{s\leq\min(h,b(u))}x_{s}/u. On 𝒟\mathcal{D} the artificial rate at v<uv<u is ∑s≤b⁡(v)𝟏[h(v)<s]/v\sum_{s\leq b(v)}\mathbf{1}[h(v)<s]/v. The term of s≤min⁡(h,b⁡(u))s\leq\min(h,b(u)) is present only for v>xsv>x_{s}, and then vanishes, since the ss best members of 𝒬\mathcal{Q} arrived by xsx_{s}; the term of h<s≤b⁡(u)h<s\leq b(u) equals 1/v1/v on (xs,u)(x_{s},u). So, on 𝒟\mathcal{D} and for every configuration of times, there is no artificial stop before uu with probability ∏h<s≤b⁡(u)xs/u\prod_{h<s\leq b(u)}x_{s}/u, and the product of the two probabilities is σ⁡(u)\sigma(u).

(ii) The set of members after uiu_{i} and their times are a function of the set of members after ui−1u_{i-1} and their times. Averaging (i), the conditional probabilities of no stop before ui−1u_{i-1} and before uiu_{i} are σ⁡(ui−1)\sigma(u_{i-1}) and σ⁡(ui)\sigma(u_{i}); their difference is the probability of a stop in cell ii, since almost surely no stop occurs exactly at a grid point.

(iii) Let uu be the relative time of ee. A proposal of ee requires u>x1u>x_{1} and no stop before uu. Given u∈(ui−1,ui]u\in(u_{i-1},u_{i}], the set of other members before uu and the times of the other members after uu, the latter has probability σ⁡(u)\sigma(u) by (i), and this conditioning refines that of (iii), because u≤uiu\leq u_{i}. Integrating over uu gives the bound aia_{i}.

(iv) Let yy be the member of rank rr, arriving at uu. It is proposed if and only if there is no stop before uu and fewer than b⁡(u)b(u) better members precede it. Given uu and the set of members preceding yy, the first event has probability σ⁡(u)\sigma(u) by (i), and the second is determined; the number of better predecessors is Bin⁡(r−1,u)\mathrm{Bin}(r-1,u). Integrating gives τr,i\tau_{r,i}, which is nonincreasing in rr because Bin⁡(r−1,u)\mathrm{Bin}(r-1,u) is stochastically increasing in rr. For a set of ss members, the proposals of distinct members in cell ii are disjoint events contained in the event of a stop in cell ii, so Ti​(s)≤βiT_{i}(s)\leq\beta_{i} by (ii). ∎

Geometric grids and stationary prices.

The time between a stop and the next grid point is idle, so fine grids are better; but Theorem A.10 has one kernel and kk families of tests for each of the N​kNk states. On a geometric grid all states with the same number of stops have, up to truncation, the same kernel, and the slack in Theorem A.10 lets one family of prices serve all of them.

Fix 0<q<10<q<1 and an integer N≥2N\geq 2, and use the truncated geometric grid

ti=1−qi(0≤i<N),tN=1,t_{i}=1-q^{i}\quad(0\leq i<N),\qquad t_{N}=1,

with a list in state (g,j)(g,j) that depends on jj only. The kernel of the state (0,j)(0,j) has relative cell ends u0,i=tiu_{0,i}=t_{i}; we call it the shared kernel of jj.

Lemma A.11 (Shift invariance).

Let g<Ng<N. For g≤i<Ng\leq i<N the relative cell ends of the state (g,j)(g,j) are ug,i=1−qi−g=u0,i−gu_{g,i}=1-q^{i-g}=u_{0,i-g}, and ug,N=1u_{g,N}=1. Hence, for g<i<Ng<i<N, the quantities βg,j,i\beta_{g,j,i}, ag,j,ia_{g,j,i}, τr,i\tau_{r,i} and Ti​(s)T_{i}(s) of the state (g,j)(g,j) equal those of the state (0,j)(0,j) for the cell i−gi-g, and PsP_{s} is the same for both states.

For i<Ni<N, ug,i=(ti−tg)/(1−tg)=(qg−qi)/qg=1−qi−gu_{g,i}=(t_{i}-t_{g})/(1-t_{g})=(q^{g}-q^{i})/q^{g}=1-q^{i-g}. The quantities of a cell depend only on the list and on the two relative cell ends of that cell, and PsP_{s} is the integral of the same function over all cells of the state, which partition (0,1](0,1]. ∎

Proof.

A computer check verifies the hypotheses of Theorem A.12 for explicit prices and bounds its right side from below, in exact rational arithmetic and in integer interval arithmetic with endpoints in 10−30​ℤ10^{-30}\mathbb{Z}, rounding every operation in the safe direction. It checks that every list is nondecreasing, positive and nonempty. The integrals are computed on the rational pseudo-cells (wi−1,wi](w_{i-1},w_{i}] with wi=10−30​Ziw_{i}=10^{-30}Z_{i} for i<Ni<N and wN=1w_{N}=1, which partition (0,1](0,1]. On a piece (l,v](l,v] of a pseudo-cell on which b⁡(u)=mb(u)=m is constant, σ⁡(u)=Cm​u−m\sigma(u)=C_{m}u^{-m}. For m=1m=1 the check uses ∫lv(1−u)r−1​u−1​𝑑u\int_{l}^{v}(1-u)^{r-1}u^{-1}du, which equals ln⁡(v/l)\ln(v/l) for r=1r=1 and satisfies the recursion obtained from (1−u)r−(1−u)r−1=−u​(1−u)r−1(1-u)^{r}-(1-u)^{r-1}=-u(1-u)^{r-1}, enclosing logarithms by the series of artanh\operatorname{artanh} with an explicit remainder. For m≥2m\geq 2 it uses the identity

with binomial distribution functions enclosed by repeated Bernoulli convolution. A true cell (u0,i−1,u0,i](u_{0,i-1},u_{0,i}] and the pseudo-cell (wi−1,wi](w_{i-1},w_{i}] differ by a set of measure at most 2⋅10−302\cdot 10^{-30}, and the integrands of Ti​(s)T_{i}(s) and aia_{i} lie in [0,s][0,s] and [0,1][0,1]; adding 2​s⋅10−302s\cdot 10^{-30} and 2⋅10−302\cdot 10^{-30} to the upper bounds on the pseudo-cells gives upper bounds on Ti​(s)T_{i}(s) for s≤R0=300s\leq R_{0}=300 and on a0,j,ia_{0,j,i}, for i<Ni<N. Since the pseudo-cells partition (0,1](0,1], summing the lower bounds over them gives lower bounds on PrP_{r}. The two-pick rule, the restart rule and the uniform-price rows are each needed for some budget in Table 2; the exempt variant is better than the uniform rows that we certified only for k≥500k\geq 500. Appendix B Monotone objectives at every budget

The explicit guarantee of Theorem 3.1 applies only to large budgets. For monotone objectives we now give explicit guarantees for every budget. They come from exact optimization over the observed prefix for k≤21k\leq 21, from a price policy that is mixed with the classical single-choice rule for 22≤k<10622\leq k<10^{6}, and from a variant of AttenuatedPricing for larger kk (Section B.3).

Throughout this appendix ff is nonnegative, monotone, and submodular, OPT=max|S|≤k⁡f⁡(S)\mathrm{OPT}=\max_{|S|\leq k}f(S), and f0=f⁡(∅)f_{0}=f(\emptyset). Since n≥kn\geq k and ff is monotone, there is an optimal set OO with |O|=k|O|=k. Every algorithm below queries f0f_{0} and works with f−f0f-f_{0}, which has the same marginals. For a guarantee ρ≤1\rho\leq 1 this is no loss: if 𝔼⁡[f⁡(A)−f0]≥ρ⁡(OPT−f0)\mathbb{E}[f(A)-f_{0}]\geq\rho(\mathrm{OPT}-f_{0}) then 𝔼​f​(A)≥ρ​OPT+(1−ρ)​f0≥ρ​OPT\mathbb{E}f(A)\geq\rho\,\mathrm{OPT}+(1-\rho)f_{0}\geq\rho\,\mathrm{OPT}. So in the proofs we may and do assume f0=0f_{0}=0. Arrival times are generated from timestamps as in Section 2. Πμ\Pi_{\mu} denotes a Poisson variable with mean μ\mu.

B.1 The exact-prefix rule

For a set SS of arrived elements let H⁡(S)H(S) be the subset of SS of size at most kk that maximizes ff, with ties broken first in favor of larger cardinality and then by a fixed total order on sets that does not depend on the arrival history. Let g⁡(S)=f⁡(H⁡(S))g(S)=f(H(S)). Since ff is monotone, |H⁡(S)|=min⁡{k,|S|}|H(S)|=\min\{k,|S|\}. An arriving element ee is a candidate if e∈H⁡(U)e\in H(U), where UU is the set of arrivals so far, including ee.

ExactPrefix(k,p)(k,p). Draw X∼Bin⁡(n,p)X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p) and reject the first XX arrivals. Afterwards, accept each candidate while fewer than kk elements have been accepted, and reject all other arrivals.

With timestamps, the rejected elements are exactly those with timestamp at most pp, so the rule accepts the first kk candidates after time pp. Its value queries can be organized so that every set of at most kk arrived elements is queried once, when its last member arrives.

The canonical choice has the outcast property: if e∈S∖H⁡(S)e\in S\setminus H(S), then H⁡(S∖{e})=H⁡(S)H(S\setminus\{e\})=H(S), because H⁡(S)H(S) is a subset of S∖{e}S\setminus\{e\} and wins against all its subsets. For e∈H⁡(S)e\in H(S) let Ke=H⁡(S∖{e})K_{e}=H(S\setminus\{e\}), de=g⁡(S)−f⁡(Ke)d_{e}=g(S)-f(K_{e}), and De=f⁡(e∣Ke)D_{e}=f(e\mid K_{e}), and let d⁡(S)=∑e∈H⁡(S)ded(S)=\sum_{e\in H(S)}d_{e} and D⁡(S)=∑e∈H⁡(S)DeD(S)=\sum_{e\in H(S)}D_{e}.

PoissonPrice(p,T,m,s)(p,T,m,s). Reject the elements with timestamp below pp (the sample S0S_{0}), and let M=maxi∈S0⁡(f⁡({i})−f0)M=\max_{i\in S_{0}}(f(\{i\})-f_{0}), or M=0M=0 if S0=∅S_{0}=\emptyset. θt=MΔ(t,Nt−)/h(t)=MeT−tℙ[Nt−+Πb⁡(T−t)≥c].\theta_{t}=M\,\Delta(t,N_{t-})/h(t)=M\,e^{T-t}\,\mathbb{P}\bigl[N_{t-}+\Pi_{b(T-t)}\geq c\bigr].

An arrival at time t≤Tt\leq T is accepted if and only if fewer than kk elements have been accepted and its marginal value with respect to the accepted set exceeds θt\theta_{t}. Later arrivals are rejected.

Record(p)(p). Order the elements by singleton value, breaking ties by independent uniform marks. Reject the elements with timestamp below pp, accept the first later arrival that has higher priority than every earlier arrival, and stop.

InsuredPrice(p,T,m,s,C¯)(p,T,m,s,\bar{C}). With probability (1−p)/(1−p+C¯)(1-p)/(1-p+\bar{C}) run PoissonPrice(p,T,m,s)(p,T,m,s), and otherwise run Record(p)(p).

The price policy uses at most n+1n+1 queries: f0f_{0}, the singletons of the sample, and one value f⁡(A∪{i})f(A\cup\{i\}) per later arrival. The record rule uses at most nn queries. The state of the price policy is the accepted set, since MM is frozen and the price depends only on N=|A|N=|A| and tt; a rejected element changes nothing.

Appendix C A better bound from fans

Lemma C.2.

Let X=h⁡(τ,z)X=h(\tau,z), where τ\tau is a uniformly random bijection between two sets of size RR, and z=(z1,…,zR)z=(z_{1},\dots,z_{R}) are independent and independent of τ\tau. The construction.

It is that of Theorem C.1, with the following changes. We take δ=12\delta=\frac{1}{2}; nothing before the last step of the proof of Theorem 7.2 uses δ<12\delta<\frac{1}{2}. We let QQ be the least multiple of h​Q0hQ_{0} with Q≥(log⁡Y)2Q\geq(\log Y)^{2}, and we put q=Q/(2​h)q=Q/(2h). We split the vertices 1,…,Rj1,\dots,R_{j} of 𝖥j\mathsf{F}_{j} into MjM_{j} consecutive blocks of hh vertices. Block pp has the vertices (p−1)​h+1,…,p​h(p-1)h+1,\dots,ph. Its boundary edge is b(p−1)​h+1b_{(p-1)h+1}, and for p=1p=1 this is the edge 0101. Its internal edges are b(p−1)​h+2,…,bp​hb_{(p-1)h+2},\dots,b_{ph}. The two boundary edges at block pp are its own and that of block p+1p+1; the latter is absent for p=Mjp=M_{j}. A uniformly random bijection assigns qq tokens per item to the MjM_{j} blocks, and an item owns all spokes of its qq blocks. The set ℬj,d\mathcal{B}_{j,d} consists of all bad edges of πd​Mj\pi_{d}M_{j} consecutive blocks, and these intervals of blocks partition [Mj][M_{j}]. Since Q0​πd=2​N!​den​(ℋN)/dQ_{0}\pi_{d}=2N!\,\mathrm{den}(\mathcal{H}_{N})/d, all these numbers are integers. As in Appendix C, Lemma 7.4, the relaxation f¯≥f\bar{f}\geq f, the paragraph on invisible roles and (9) carry over.

Fix j>Nj>N and write n=njn=n_{j}, M=MjM=M_{j}, R=RjR=R_{j}. Let tat_{a} be the time of item aa of level jj, let UpU_{p} be the time of the owner of block pp, and let ziz_{i} be the carrier time of bib_{i}. As in Appendix C, the ziz_{i} are independent and uniform, and they are independent of the bijection and of (ta)(t_{a}); 𝒯j\mathcal{T}_{j}, ϵj\epsilon_{j} and λℓ\lambda_{\ell} are as there. Lemma C.11 (Local facts).

Let pp be a block with owner time tt, and let ee be a boundary edge at pp, between pp and p′=p+op^{\prime}=p+o with o=±1o=\pm 1, with carrier time VV.

  1. (a)

    Every internal edge of pp in 𝒯j\mathcal{T}_{j} has carrier time less than tt.

  2. (b)

    If e∈𝒯je\in\mathcal{T}_{j}, then V<tV<t or Up′>VU_{p^{\prime}}>V. Moreover e∉𝒯je\notin\mathcal{T}_{j} on each of the following events. W1W_{1}: V<tV<t, Up−1,Up+1<VU_{p-1},U_{p+1}<V, and the hh bad edges on the path from the endpoint of ee in pp through pp to block p−op-o arrive before VV. W2W_{2}: t<V<Up′t<V<U_{p^{\prime}}, Up+2​o<VU_{p+2o}<V, and the hh bad edges on the path from the endpoint of ee in p′p^{\prime} through p′p^{\prime} to block p+2​op+2o arrive before VV.

  3. (c)

    Let ee be a boundary edge between blocks with owner times t,ut,u. Then e∈𝒯je\in\mathcal{T}_{j} if t>Vt>V and the internal edge of the left block at ee arrives after VV, or if t<V<ut<V<u and the internal edge of the right block at ee arrives after VV.

  4. (d)

    If both boundary edges at pp arrive after tt, then every internal edge of pp that arrives before tt lies in 𝒯j\mathcal{T}_{j}. Moreover, for every set SS of atoms of 𝖥j\mathsf{F}_{j} that arrive before tt, deleting the internal edges of pp from SS does not change φ𝖥j​(S)\varphi_{\mathsf{F}_{j}}(S).

If the owner times involved are distinct independent uniform variables, independent of the carrier times, then, conditionally on tt (and on uu in (c)), the event in the first part of (b) has probability 1+t22\frac{1+t^{2}}{2} and W1∪W2W_{1}\cup W_{2} has probability ϑ⁡(t)\vartheta(t). The event in (c) has probability w−w22w-\frac{w^{2}}{2} with w=max⁡(t,u)w=\max(t,u), and the hypothesis of (d) has probability (1−t)2(1-t)^{2}.

Proof.

(a) After time tt, both endpoints are joined to 00 by spokes. (b) If V>tV>t and Up′<VU_{p^{\prime}}<V, the same holds for ee. On W1W_{1}, the endpoint of ee in p′p^{\prime} is joined to 00 by its spoke, and the other endpoint is joined to 00 through block pp and the spoke of a vertex of block p−op-o. On W2W_{2}, the endpoint in pp is joined to 00 by its spoke, and the other endpoint through p′p^{\prime} and block p+2​op+2o. Neither path uses ee. (c) The endpoint in question has no spoke and no other bad edge before VV, so it is isolated in G<VG_{<V}. (d) Before tt, no spoke of pp and no boundary edge at pp has arrived. So the internal edges of pp in SS form a forest on the vertices of pp that meets no other edge of SS, and each of them adds one to the rank. For the probabilities, integrate over V=sV=s: the integrands are 𝟏[s<t]+𝟏[s>t](1−s)\mathbf{1}[s<t]+\mathbf{1}[s>t](1-s); 𝟏[s<t]sh+2+𝟏[s>t](1−s)sh+1\mathbf{1}[s<t]s^{h+2}+\mathbf{1}[s>t](1-s)s^{h+1}; (1−s)𝟏[s<max(t,u)](1-s)\mathbf{1}[s<\max(t,u)]. The events W1W_{1} and W2W_{2} are disjoint. ∎

Lemma C.13 (Baseline).

𝔼⁡[R−|𝒯j|]≤R⁡(βh+o⁡(1))\mathbb{E}[R-|\mathcal{T}_{j}|]\leq R(\beta_{h}+o(1)).

Proof.

A bad edge bib_{i} arriving at time ss is outside 𝒯j\mathcal{T}_{j} exactly when both its endpoints are joined to 00 in G<sG_{<s}. In a doubly infinite chain of blocks with independent uniform times, an endpoint is joined to 00 on its side with probability v⁡(s)v(s). Indeed, its block is rooted with probability ss, and otherwise its hh bad edges towards the next block must all have arrived. A boundary edge is therefore outside 𝒯j\mathcal{T}_{j} with probability v​(s)2v(s)^{2}. An internal edge is outside 𝒯j\mathcal{T}_{j} with probability s+(1−s)​sh​v​(s)2s+(1-s)s^{h}v(s)^{2}, where shs^{h} accounts for the other hh edges of the path between the neighbouring blocks. Averaging over the hh positions gives βh\beta_{h}. In the fan, fix A≥1A\geq 1 and an edge whose block is at distance more than AA from both ends. The 2​A+12A+1 blocks around it have distinct owners with probability at least 1−(2​A+1)2/n1-(2A+1)^{2}/n. Exploring at most AA unrooted blocks on each side changes the probability by at most 2​(1−s)A​sh​A≤2​(h+1)−A2(1-s)^{A}s^{hA}\leq 2(h+1)^{-A}. Let Y→∞Y\to\infty and then A→∞A\to\infty, as in Lemma C.5. ∎

Lemma C.14 (Rejected blocks).

𝔼⁡[|VZ|−IZ−BZ]≥R⁡(𝔼​∫γh​d​λj−o⁡(1))\mathbb{E}\bigl[|V_{Z}|-I_{Z}-B_{Z}\bigr]\geq R\bigl(\mathbb{E}\int\gamma_{h}\,d\lambda_{j}-o(1)\bigr).

Fix an item aa. Let CaC_{a} be the number of internal edges of its qq blocks that arrive before tat_{a}.
